title: Arabic Coffee
description: Saudi (Arabic) coffee is made from lightly roasted beans boiled in a pot, then poured into the dallah over cardamom, saffron and cloves, and served in small finjans with dates; it is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Our version has no sugar and no coffee creamer or milk powder, with a moderate portion of dates.
ingredients: 3 tbsp lightly roasted Arabic coffee, medium ground (30 g)
steps: Bring the water to the boil in the coffee pot (mulgama), then turn the heat down to low.
Add the coffee, stir once and let it simmer gently for 12–15 minutes without boiling over.
Turn off the heat, cover and leave 3–5 minutes so the grounds settle to the bottom.
Put the cardamom, saffron and cloves in the dallah or flask, then pour the coffee over them slowly, leaving the grounds behind.
Leave 2 minutes to infuse, then serve in finjans with the dates.
hints: What changed: no sugar, coffee creamer or milk powder (which some modern versions add), and the portion is 3 finjans with 2 small dates instead of sweets on the side.
Kidney tip: the coffee itself is low in potassium at this amount, but dates are high in potassium; keep to 2 dates at most and count the coffee in your daily fluid allowance if you have one.

Diabetes and blood pressure tip: one serving has about 13 g carbohydrate, all from the dates; do not go above 2 dates, and limit yourself to 3–4 finjans a day as caffeine can raise blood pressure for a while.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Saudipedia, Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Qurs Al-Mulla Bread
description: Qurs al-mulla, also called qurs al-jamr, is an old Bedouin Saudi bread of whole-wheat flour, water and salt, buried in hot ash and embers until cooked, then crumbled and dressed with ghee. This home version bakes the loaf in the oven or a covered cast-iron pot, uses a measured amount of ghee and a little honey instead of sugar.
serving_size: 1 portion of crumbled bread with ghee (about 85 g)
ingredients: 1½ tbsp honey (30 g) to serve, optional
steps: Mix the flour with the salt, add the water little by little and knead for 8–10 minutes to a firm dough that does not stick to your hands; cover and rest for 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 230 °C with a cast-iron tray or baking stone inside for at least 20 minutes.
Press the dough by hand into a thick round about 22–25 cm wide and 2 cm thick and prick it with a fork.

Put the round on the hot tray and bake for 35–40 minutes, turning it halfway, until browned on both sides and hollow-sounding when tapped. (Outdoors it is traditionally buried in ash and embers for about an hour, then brushed clean.)
Brush off any burnt crust, then crumble the hot bread by hand or cut it into small pieces in the serving dish.
Melt the ghee and pour it over the crumbs while tossing, drizzle with honey if you like and serve warm.
hints: What changed: whole-wheat flour, limited salt (½ g per portion), far less ghee than usual (under 1 tsp per portion), and a little optional honey instead of sugar.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour has more phosphorus and potassium than white flour; you can swap half of it for white flour and keep to one portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 40 g carbohydrate; skip the honey and serve it with low-fat laban or a boiled egg and salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Al Watan (Saudi newspaper), Al Khaleej magazine

title: Chicken in Foil
description: Chicken in foil (qasdeer) is a popular home and camping dish: chicken pieces with onion, tomato, peppers, mixed vegetables and chickpeas are seasoned, sealed in foil and cooked on the stove or embers until tender in their own juices. Here the chicken is skinless, homemade unsalted stock replaces the stock cube, and only one spoon of olive oil and little salt are used.
serving_size: 1 plate of chicken and vegetables (about 400 g)
ingredients: 300 g skinless chicken breast, cut into large pieces
300 g skinless boneless chicken thighs, cut up
250 g frozen mixed vegetables (peas and carrots)
120 g canned chickpeas, drained and well rinsed
1 tsp curry powder, 1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
120 ml homemade unsalted chicken stock or hot water
steps: In a large bowl mix the chicken with the onion, tomatoes, pepper, frozen vegetables, chickpeas and garlic.
Whisk the lemon juice, oil, spices and salt into the stock, pour it over the chicken and vegetables and toss well to coat.
Lay two sheets of foil crosswise in a wide pot or tray, pile the mixture in the centre and seal the foil tightly on all sides so no steam escapes.
Cook the parcel in the pot over low heat for 50–60 minutes (or in the oven at 200 °C for 45–50 minutes, or on embers) until the chicken is fully cooked.
Open the foil carefully to avoid the steam, check the chicken is cooked through, and serve hot with salad or a small amount of basmati rice or bread.
hints: What changed: no Maggi cube (homemade unsalted stock and spices instead), skinless chicken, one spoon of oil for the whole dish, and rinsed canned chickpeas to cut sodium.
Kidney tip: chickpeas, tomato and peas contain potassium and phosphorus; you can leave out or halve the chickpeas, swap the tomato for courgette or cabbage, and keep to 90–120 g chicken.
Diabetes tip: one portion has only about 22 g carbohydrate; if serving with rice, keep to about 75 g cooked basmati rice with salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookpad Saudi Arabia, Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Qursan
description: Qursan is a Najdi dish in which thin, dried whole-wheat flatbread (qursan bread) is broken up and layered with a meat and vegetable broth and onion with dried lime until it soaks it all up. In this version the bread is made at home from whole-wheat flour without fat, with lean meat, plenty of vegetables and a little olive oil, no sugar, apricot paste or butter on top, and less salt.
ingredients: 200 g whole-wheat flour, a pinch of salt (1 g) and about 130 ml water (or 200 g ready-made dried whole-wheat qursan)
560 g lean lamb leg, cut in small pieces
1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp black pepper, 2 pierced dried limes, 3 cardamom pods
1 carrot (100 g), 1 zucchini (150 g), 1 small eggplant (150 g), 200 g pumpkin and 100 g green beans, cubed
1 medium onion, finely chopped (100 g), with 1 tsp ground dried lime, ½ tsp cinnamon and a pinch each of cardamom and turmeric
steps: For the qursan bread: knead the flour, salt and water until smooth, rest for 30 minutes, then divide into 4 balls and roll each out very thin.
Cook each sheet on a hot dry saj or pan for 1–2 minutes per side until dry and speckled, then let it cool and break it into pieces about half the size of your palm.
For the broth: heat the oil in a pot and soften the onion, then add the meat and stir until it changes colour; add the spices, tomatoes and tomato paste and let it thicken for 5 minutes.
Pour in the boiling water, add the dried limes and chillies and simmer on medium heat for 45 minutes until the meat is almost tender (or 25 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Add the carrot, then after 5 minutes the rest of the vegetables and the salt, and cook for 15–20 minutes until tender; then lift the meat out and set aside.

Heat the oven to 180°C. In an ovenproof pot or deep dish put a little broth, then a layer of qursan, then broth with vegetables, then some of the onion and dried lime; repeat until everything is used.
Push a spoon down into the layers in several places so the broth reaches all the bread, arrange the meat in the centre, cover with foil and bake for 25–30 minutes until the broth is absorbed.
Sprinkle with spring onion and serve hot.
hints: What changed: homemade fat-free whole-wheat qursan, no sugar, apricot paste or browned butter on top, lean meat, little oil, more vegetables and about half the usual salt; dried lime, cinnamon and cardamom replace the date-based masmana spice.

Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour, pumpkin, tomatoes, tomato paste, carrot and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one plate, and you can halve the pumpkin and tomatoes and use more zucchini and green beans. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 57 g carbohydrate with 11 g fibre; the qursan is the starch of the meal, so do not add bread or rice, and add a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Qursan), Saudipedia (Qursan)

title: Hijazi Sulat Lahm
description: Sulat is a popular Hijazi dish from Medina and Makkah: lamb pieces slowly cooked with onion, garlic, cumin and black pepper until the sauce thickens, served with thin bread. This version uses lean lamb leg instead of rendered fat and ghee, two teaspoons of olive oil, little salt, whole-wheat bread and a fresh salad.
serving_size: 1 plate of meat in sauce with bread and salad (about 380 g)
ingredients: 520 g lean boneless lamb leg, cut into small cubes, visible fat trimmed
1 medium onion, grated or finely chopped (150 g)
200 g small onions (whole baby onions, peeled)
1–2 hot green chillies, chopped (15 g), to taste
1 tsp ground cumin, ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp turmeric (hurd), 1 tsp mixed spices (bezar)
2 cucumbers (200 g) and 1 tomato (150 g), diced
juice of ½ lemon (20 ml) and a small pinch of salt (1 g) for the salad
steps: Heat the oil in a non-stick pot over medium-high heat, add the grated onion and stir for 4–5 minutes until soft and lightly golden.
Add the garlic and green chilli and stir for 1 minute, then add the cumin, black pepper, turmeric and spices and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the lamb and stir over high heat until it changes colour and its juices have almost evaporated (about 10 minutes).
Add the boiling water and the small onions, cover, lower the heat and simmer gently for 1–1¼ hours, stirring now and then, until the meat is tender and the sauce has reduced and thickened.
Add the salt at the end and taste; if the sauce is still thin, uncover and cook 10 more minutes.
Toss the cucumber and tomato with the lemon juice and pinch of salt, and serve the sulat hot with the thin bread and salad.
hints: What changed: lean lamb leg instead of rendering pieces of fat, 2 tsp olive oil for the whole pot, little salt added at the end, and whole-wheat bread with a fresh salad.
Kidney tip: meat and tomato contain phosphorus and potassium; keep to 90–100 g cooked meat, spoon less sauce onto the bread, and you can replace the tomato with extra cucumber.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 34 g carbohydrate, mostly from the bread; keep to one small flatbread and fill up on salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Dagoos Tomato Sauce
description: Dagoos is a spicy Saudi sauce of tomato, chilli, garlic and lemon served beside kabsa and mandi. This version has no ketchup or stock cubes, uses no-salt-added tomato paste and very little salt.
ingredients: 2 green chillies (20 g) and 1 red chilli (10 g), seeded if you like
½ tsp cumin, ¼ tsp kabsa spice mix
steps: Blend the tomatoes, chillies and garlic until smooth.
Pour into a small pan over medium heat, add the tomato paste, cumin, kabsa spices and water, bring to the boil, then simmer for 10 minutes until slightly thick.
Add the olive oil, lemon juice, vinegar and salt and stir for 3 minutes over low heat.
Take off the heat, stir in the parsley and serve warm or cold beside kabsa. Keep in a closed jar in the fridge for up to 4 days.
hints: What changed: no ketchup (high in sugar and salt) and no stock cubes, no-salt-added tomato paste, one spoon of oil instead of a lot, and sourness from lemon and vinegar instead of salt.
Kidney tip: tomatoes are high in potassium; keep to 2 tablespoons of dagoos with the meal, and you can replace half the tomatoes with roasted red sweet pepper.
Diabetes tip: dagoos is low in carbohydrate (about 7 g per portion) and its flavour helps you eat a smaller amount of rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (Saudi dagoos), Atyab Tabkha (spicy dagoos for kabsa)

title: Hijazi Meat Mu'arraq
description: Mu'arraq is a Madinah and Hijazi dish of meat browned with cardamom and mastic, then slowly simmered in tomato and onion sauce until tender, served with white rice. We used lean leg meat, 1 tsp ghee with olive oil, and less no-salt-added tomato paste.
ingredients: 500 g lean lamb leg, cut in medium cubes
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) and 1 tsp ghee (4.5 g)
3 cardamom pods and 5 small mastic grains
½ tsp mixed spices, ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp chilli powder
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
¼ tsp salt (1.5 g) and 400 ml water
steps: Heat the oil and ghee in a pot over medium heat with the cardamom and mastic until fragrant.
Add the meat and stir until it browns, releases its juices and they dry up.
Add the onion, garlic and tomato paste and stir for 3 minutes, then add the blended tomatoes and cook until most of their liquid has evaporated.
Add the spices, salt and hot water, cover and simmer on low heat for 1 hour until the meat is tender and the sauce is thick.
Meanwhile bring the rice water and salt to the boil, add the drained rice, cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes.
Serve the mu'arraq on or beside the rice with a green salad.
hints: What changed: lean leg meat instead of fatty meat on the bone, 1 tsp ghee instead of 2 tbsp, half the tomato paste and no salt added, and a set rice portion.
Kidney tip: tomato paste, tomatoes and meat are high in potassium and phosphorus; you can leave out the paste, and keep to one portion of meat (about 90 g cooked) with a little sauce.
Diabetes tip: the plate has about 48 g carbohydrate from the rice; start with the salad, and you can swap a third of the rice for brown rice or serve it with whole-wheat bread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Yummy (Layalina), Sho Tabkha

title: Southern Areeka
description: Areeka is a traditional sweet from southern Saudi Arabia (Asir and Al-Baha): a whole-wheat dough is baked, kneaded while hot and served with ghee, honey and dates alongside Arabic coffee. This version uses toasted whole-wheat flour, a small amount of ghee, half the usual honey with dates for sweetness, and a small portion.
ingredients: 1 tsp ghee for greasing the pan (5 g)
steps: Toast the whole-wheat flour in a dry pot over low heat for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until it smells nutty, then let it cool a little.
Add the salt, then the warm water gradually, and mix to a soft dough a little thicker than cake batter; rest it for 15 minutes.

Grease a non-stick pan or tray with the first teaspoon of ghee, spread the dough in it and bake in an oven heated to 200 °C for about 30 minutes, or cook over low heat, turning once, until done on both sides.
While it is hot, put the bread in a clean bag or bowl and knead it with your hands (protected with a cloth) until smooth and cohesive. Add a spoonful of hot water if it gets dry.
Shape it in a serving bowl, make a well in the centre, pour the melted ghee into it, drizzle the honey around the edge and decorate with the dates.
Divide into 6 small portions and serve warm with Arabic coffee.
hints: What changed: whole-wheat flour instead of white, about 2.5 g ghee per portion instead of large amounts, half the usual honey with dates for sweetness, and small portions.

Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour and dates have more phosphorus and potassium than white flour; keep to one portion, and you can swap half the whole-wheat flour for white flour and use one date per portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 42 g carbohydrate; count it in your meal, have it with unsweetened coffee and do not add extra honey.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Yummy Layalina, Bayut

title: Hasawi Goat Mandi
description: Hasawi mandi is a celebrated dish of Al-Ahsa for feasts and Eid: goat cooks above a pot of rice in a pit oven and is smoked with palm-frond bases. This is a home oven version with lean goat, a little ghee and less salt.
ingredients: 600 g goat meat from leg or shoulder, visible fat trimmed, in large pieces
1 tsp mixed spices, ¼ tsp ground saffron soaked in 2 tbsp water
200 g long-grain basmati rice, washed and soaked 30 minutes
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) and 2 tsp ghee (9 g)
Whole spices: 5 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cloves, 1 pierced dried lime (loomi)
¾ tsp salt (4 g), split between meat and rice
1 piece of charcoal or a small piece of dry palm-frond base for smoking (optional)
steps: Rub the goat with the spices and ¼ tsp of the salt, sprinkle with the saffron water and leave 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 170°C. In an ovenproof pot, soften the onion in the oil and ghee, then add the tomato, bell pepper, chilli and whole spices.
Add the drained rice, the rest of the salt and the water, stir once, then seal the pot with foil and pierce several holes in it.

Start the meat alone: put it on the oven rack over a tray, tent with foil and cook 1¼ hours, then set the rice pot on the lowest shelf right under the meat so its juices drip through the pierced foil.
Cook 45 minutes more until the meat is tender and the rice has absorbed the water, then uncover the meat and brown it for 10 minutes.

For the Hasawi flavour: place the lit charcoal or palm-frond piece in a metal bowl inside the switched-off oven with the rice and meat, close for 5 minutes, then open the door carefully to let the smoke out.
Serve the rice topped with the goat, with green salad and low-fat laban.
hints: What changed: goat is naturally lean and visible fat is trimmed, only 2 tsp ghee, no stock cubes and much less salt.
Kidney tip: goat, tomato and peppers add potassium; keep to 90–100 g cooked meat and you can halve the tomato.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 46 g carbohydrate; serve with a large salad and you can mix a quarter brown rice into the rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Al-Madina newspaper (Hasawi mandi), Arabic Wikipedia (Mandi)

title: Okra and Meat Stew
description: Okra with meat is an everyday stew in Saudi homes: meat is cooked in tomato sauce, then okra tossed with a garlic and coriander fry is added, and it is served with rice. This version uses lean lamb, far less oil, no-salt-added tomato paste and no stock cubes.
ingredients: 500 g lean lamb leg, cut in medium pieces
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), ½ tsp cumin and ½ ground dried lime (loomi)
1 small bunch fresh coriander, chopped (30 g)
500 g small okra, fresh or frozen
steps: Trim visible fat from the meat. Heat the tablespoon of oil in a pot and cook the onion until golden.
Add the meat and turn until browned on all sides, then add the tomato, paste, spices, cumin, dried lime and 500 ml hot water.
Cover and simmer for about 1 hour until the meat is nearly tender, adding a little water if needed.
For the fry: heat the oil in a pan and stir the garlic for 30 seconds, add the fresh and ground coriander, then the okra, and toss for 3–4 minutes.
Add the okra mixture to the meat with the salt and simmer for 15–20 minutes until the okra is tender and the sauce has thickened.
Add the lemon juice and serve hot with rice.
hints: What changed: lean, trimmed lamb, much less oil than usual, okra tossed in the garlic fry rather than fried, and no-salt tomato paste with no stock cubes.
Kidney tip: okra, tomato and tomato paste are high in potassium; use only 2 tomatoes, boil the okra and discard the water before the fry, and keep to a small plate with white rice.
Diabetes tip: the stew itself has about 20 g carbohydrate; serve it with 150 g cooked rice, ideally brown rice or half bulgur.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, WebTeb

title: Southern Fatta with Ghee and Honey
description: Southern fatta is a traditional breakfast from the south of Saudi Arabia (Asir, Al-Baha and Najran): wholewheat griddle breads torn into pieces and dressed with basil-scented ghee and honey. This version uses less than 1 tsp ghee per serving, no sugar in the dough and less honey.
ingredients: 1 tsp olive oil to wipe the griddle (4.5 g)
1 small bunch basil, washed and dried (10 g)
steps: Mix the flour with the nigella seeds and salt, then whisk in the water gradually to a batter slightly thicker than cake batter. Leave it to rest for 30 minutes.
Heat a griddle or non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little of the oil on kitchen paper.
Pour in a ladle of batter and spread it into a thin round. Cook until browned underneath, flip and brown the other side. Repeat with the rest of the batter.

For the basil ghee: toast the spoon of flour in a small pan over low heat until golden and fragrant. Add the ghee; when it melts and starts to foam, add the basil, cover for under a minute, then turn off the heat, let it cool a little and strain.
Tear the warm breads by hand into medium pieces in a serving dish.
Pour the basil ghee and then the honey over the bread and serve warm with low-fat milk, tea or coffee.
hints: What changed: all the flour is wholewheat, the sugar in the dough is gone, 25 g ghee serves six instead of a whole block of butter, and the honey is cut to 10 g per serving.
Kidney tip: wholewheat flour has more phosphorus and potassium than white flour; you can use half wholewheat and half white flour, keep to one portion, and drink tea or light coffee instead of milk.

Diabetes tip: one portion has about 45 g carbohydrate including 8 g added sugar; serve the honey on the side and use little, and eat a boiled egg or low-fat laban with it to slow the rise in blood sugar.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Saudipedia (Asir folk foods), Mawdoo3

title: Hasawi Kubba
description: Hasawi kubba are patties of soaked, ground hareis wheat filled with onion, parsley and coriander, first boiled and then browned; they are a traditional starter in Al-Ahsa for breakfast and Ramadan. This version browns them on a griddle brushed with oil or in the oven instead of deep frying, with little salt.
ingredients: 300 g hareis wheat, soaked in water 6 hours and well drained
70 g flour (white or half wholewheat), plus a little for rolling
½ tsp cumin, ¼ tsp turmeric
1 large onion, very finely chopped and squeezed dry (150 g)
¼ bunch fresh coriander, chopped (15 g)
¼ tsp black pepper, a pinch of salt (0.5 g)
1 tbsp olive oil for brushing (13.5 g)
steps: Grind the soaked wheat in a food processor or mincer until fine, then add the flour, cumin, turmeric and salt and knead into a sticky, firm dough.
Mix the filling ingredients.
Divide the dough into 12 balls, flatten each by hand on a floured surface, put a tablespoon of filling in the centre, gather the edges to seal, then flatten again into a thick disc about 9 cm across.
Bring a large pot of unsalted water to the boil, drop the discs in one at a time and lift them out with a slotted spoon once they float (about 1 minute); leave to dry on a rack.
Heat a griddle or non-stick pan, brush the discs lightly with oil and brown for 3–4 minutes on each side until golden and crisp (or bake at 220 °C for 15–20 minutes, turning once).
Serve hot with lemon and a green salad. The boiled discs can be frozen, each wrapped separately, and browned when needed.
hints: What changed: browned with a brush of oil on a griddle or in the oven instead of deep frying, boiled in unsalted water, and no processed or cheddar cheese in the dough, with little salt.
Kidney tip: whole wheat is high in phosphorus and potassium; you can replace part of the wheat with extra white flour, and keep to one or two patties with a low-protein meal.
Diabetes tip: two patties have about 47 g carbohydrate from fibre-rich whole grain; count them instead of bread or rice in the meal and serve with salad and low-fat laban.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Atyab Tabkha (Hasawi kubba), Al-Yaum newspaper (making Hasawi kubba)

title: Kamouniya
description: Kamouniya is a popular Saudi dish, well known in the Hijaz, in which cleaned lamb tripe is cooked with onion, tomato, green chilli and plenty of cumin. This version leaves out the lamb fat, uses one spoon of olive oil and little salt, and adds a few lentils.
ingredients: 600 g cleaned lamb tripe, fat trimmed
2 tbsp white vinegar, juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp cumin seeds
2 cinnamon sticks, 2 bay leaves, 1 tsp turmeric, 5 garlic cloves
1 tbsp ground cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp ground cardamom
A handful of chopped fresh coriander (20 g)
steps: Wash the tripe well, cover it with water in a pot with the vinegar, lemon juice and cumin seeds, boil for 10 minutes and discard the water.

Return it to the pot with fresh water, the cinnamon, bay leaves, turmeric and garlic and simmer until tender (about 30 minutes, or 15 minutes in a pressure cooker), then drain and cut into thin strips.
Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the tripe and crushed garlic and stir for 3 minutes.
Add the spices, tomatoes and chillies and stir until the tomatoes break down.
Add the lentils, 300 ml hot water and the salt, cover and cook on very low heat for 30 minutes until the tripe and lentils are soft and the sauce thickens.
Stir in the fresh coriander for the last 2 minutes and serve with lemon, spring onion, rocket and whole-wheat bread.
hints: What changed: no lamb fat and no stock cubes, a single spoon of olive oil, trimmed tripe, and little salt with plenty of cumin and coriander.

Kidney tip: tripe has less phosphorus than liver or heart, but offal is high in cholesterol and purines; leave out the liver, keep to one portion, and you can omit the lentils to lower potassium and phosphorus.
Diabetes and heart tip: the dish is low in carbohydrate (about 18 g); pick one small whole-wheat bread, and have it no more than once a week because of its cholesterol.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Mawdoo3, Elwasfa

title: Fish Maqluba
description: Fish maqluba is a coastal version of maqluba made in Saudi and Gulf homes: a base of onion, tomato, carrot and pepper, then fish pieces, then rice, turned upside down to serve. In this version the fish is oven-baked instead of fried, with little oil, no stock cubes and limited salt.
ingredients: 600 g white fish fillet (hamour or similar), in large pieces
½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp curry powder, ½ tsp turmeric, ¼ tsp black pepper
½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp curry powder, ¼ tsp black pepper
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 15 minutes
Whole spices: 3 cardamom pods, 2 bay leaves
About 450 ml boiling water or homemade unsalted fish stock
steps: Season the fish with the lemon juice and spices and leave for at least 30 minutes. Heat the oven to 200°C.
Brush a tray with the teaspoon of oil, lay the fish on it and bake for 10 minutes until firm but not fully cooked.
Heat the tablespoon of oil in a deep pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the tomato and spices and stir for 2 minutes.
Add the carrot and bell pepper, cover and cook on low heat for 5 minutes until soft, then spread them over the bottom of the pot.
Lay the fish over the vegetables, then spread the drained rice and whole spices on top.
Dissolve the salt in the boiling water or stock and pour it in gently until it is about 1 cm above the rice; bring to the boil, then cover and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes.
Rest for 10 minutes, then turn it out onto a platter and scatter the almonds on top. Serve with a green salad.
hints: What changed: the fish is baked instead of fried, there is less oil in the vegetable base, no stock cubes, and about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: fish, tomato, carrot and almonds provide potassium and phosphorus; you can leave out the almonds and use less tomato, and keep to one portion (about 110 g cooked fish and 150 g cooked rice). Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 50 g carbohydrate; start with the salad, and you can replace a quarter of the rice with soaked brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Wikipedia (Maqluba), Elbalad (fish fillet maqluba)

title: Fattoush
description: Fattoush is a Levantine salad of lettuce, cucumber, tomato, peppers and herbs with crisp bread and a lemon-sumac dressing, and it is common on Saudi tables. In this version whole-wheat bread is toasted in the oven instead of fried, with less oil and salt.
ingredients: 1 green bell pepper (100 g) and 1 red bell pepper (100 g), chopped
4 radishes, sliced (60 g) and 3 spring onions (40 g)
30 g parsley and 10 g fresh mint, chopped
1 small whole-wheat pita (60 g), cut into squares
2 tbsp lemon juice (30 g) and 1 tbsp vinegar (15 g)
1 tsp sumac, ¼ tsp cumin, 1 small garlic clove, crushed (3 g)
steps: Spread the bread squares on a tray and toast them in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes until crisp.
Put the lettuce, cucumber, tomato, peppers, radishes, spring onions, parsley and mint in a large bowl.
Whisk the olive oil with the lemon juice, vinegar, sumac, cumin, garlic and salt until slightly thick.
Pour the dressing over the vegetables and toss, then add the toasted bread just before serving and dust with a little sumac.
hints: What changed: the bread is whole wheat and oven-toasted instead of fried, olive oil is 5 g per serving, and salt is ½ g per serving, with sumac and lemon carrying the flavour.
Kidney tip: tomatoes and parsley contain potassium; you can replace half the tomatoes with cucumber and peppers, and use white bread instead of whole wheat to lower phosphorus.
Diabetes tip: fattoush is low in carbohydrate and high in fibre, a good way to fill half the plate next to rice or grilled meat.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia, Sayidaty

title: Hail Madhbi (Salt-Pot Lamb)
description: Madhbi is meat cooked by the heat of hot stones or hot coarse salt in a tightly sealed pot; in Hail, young lamb is cooked on a bed of hot coarse salt and served on spiced rice. In this version the meat sits on foil so it does not take up the salt, and it uses lean leg meat, a little olive oil and limited salt.
ingredients: About 1.5 kg coarse salt (for heat only; it is not eaten and does not touch the meat)
650 g lean young lamb leg, cut in large pieces (boneless weight)
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
1 tsp olive oil (4.5 g) and 1 tsp ghee (4.5 g)
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 2 bay leaves
steps: Mix the meat with the lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, spices and the ¼ tsp salt, and leave for at least 30 minutes.
Put the coarse salt in a heavy, thick pot to a depth of 3–4 cm and heat it over medium-low heat for about 15 minutes until very hot and lightly crackling.
Lay a double sheet of foil with a few small holes over the salt, then arrange the meat on it so it touches neither the salt nor the sides of the pot.
Seal the top of the pot tightly with foil and then the lid, and cook on low heat for about 1½ hours without opening, until the meat is tender and browned.
Meanwhile heat the oil and ghee in another pot, cook the onion until soft, then add the whole spices, tomato and chilli and stir for 3 minutes.
Add the boiling water and salt, then the drained rice; boil until the water drops to the level of the rice, then cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes.
Lift the meat gently off the foil and place it on the rice; discard the salt once cool (it can be reused for cooking only). Serve with a green salad.
hints: What changed: traditionally the meat sits directly on the salt and absorbs some of it; here foil separates them so the salt only supplies heat, and the meat is trimmed of visible fat, with olive oil instead of fat.

Kidney tip: meat and tomato provide potassium and phosphorus; keep to one portion (about 110 g cooked meat and 150 g cooked rice), and you can leave the tomato out of the rice. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 45 g carbohydrate; start with the salad, and you can replace a quarter of the rice with soaked brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (madhbi lahm), Khaleej Kitchen (stone madhbi), Elbalad (salt madhbi)

title: Chicken Marqooq
description: A version of Najdi marqooq in which spiced whole-wheat dough sheets are cooked with chicken and mixed vegetables in a tomato broth. This version uses skinless chicken, a little olive oil and more vegetables, with no stock cubes and less salt.
ingredients: a pinch of salt (1 g), ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp ground coriander, ¼ tsp garlic powder, a pinch each of cinnamon and black pepper
300 g skinless chicken breast, cut in large pieces
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cloves, 1 bay leaf, 1 pierced dried lime; plus 1 tsp bezar and ½ tsp turmeric
1 small eggplant, cut in pieces (150 g)
1 green bell pepper, cut in pieces (100 g)
steps: Mix the flour with the salt and spices, add the water gradually and knead until the dough holds together, then cover for 20 minutes and divide into 8 balls.
Soak the potato cubes in warm water for 2 hours, then drain (to lower the potassium).
Heat the oil in a wide pot and cook the onion until soft and lightly coloured, then add the whole spices and garlic for 1 minute.
Add the chicken and stir until it turns white and the edges colour, then add the carrot, eggplant, bell pepper, tomato paste, bezar and turmeric and stir for 3 minutes.
Pour in the boiling water and simmer on medium heat for 20 minutes.
Roll each ball very thin on a floured surface and add the sheets to the boiling broth one at a time, stirring gently after each so they do not stick.
Add the zucchini, potato and salt, cover and cook on low heat for 25 minutes until the dough and vegetables are tender, then serve hot.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes, skinless chicken, little oil, a small amount of soaked potato and about half the usual salt with more vegetables.

Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour, potato, carrot, tomato paste and chicken are high in potassium and phosphorus; soak the potato as in the steps or replace it with zucchini, and keep to one plate with only a little broth. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 62 g carbohydrate; you can leave out the potato to lower it, do not add bread or rice, and start with a green salad.
Best kept as an occasional dish for kidney, diabetes and heart diets; keep to one serving.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), WebTeb (chicken marqooq), Arabic Wikipedia (Marqooq)

title: Oven Chicken Mandi
description: Mandi is a rice and meat dish from Hadramawt that is now popular across Saudi Arabia: the chicken cooks above the rice so its juices drip down, then it is smoked with charcoal. This is a home oven version with skinless chicken, little oil and less salt.
ingredients: 1 chicken (about 1.1 kg), skin removed and halved (about 600 g edible meat)
1 tsp mandi spice mix, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp cumin
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 30 minutes
Whole spices: 4 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 dried lime, 2 bay leaves, 5 black peppercorns
¾ tsp salt (4 g), split between chicken and rice
1 small piece of charcoal for smoking (optional)
steps: Mix the lemon juice, garlic, ground spices, the chicken oil and ¼ tsp of the salt; rub the chicken inside and out and leave 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180°C. In a pot, soften the onion in the rice oil, then add the whole spices, chilli, the rest of the salt and the boiling water and boil 5 minutes.
Spread the drained rice in a deep oven tray, pour the spiced liquid with the onion over it and level without pressing.
Seal the tray with two layers of foil and pierce several holes, then lay the chicken on the foil and cover it with another sheet of foil.
Bake 1¼–1½ hours until the chicken is cooked (75°C at the thickest part) and the rice is tender, then uncover the chicken and brown it under the grill for 5 minutes.
To smoke: put the glowing charcoal in a small metal bowl beside the chicken, cover the tray for 3 minutes, then remove the charcoal.
Serve the rice topped with the chicken, with salad and a homemade unsalted hot tomato salsa.
hints: What changed: skin removed, a lemon and garlic marinade instead of salty paste, no stock cubes and only 2 tbsp oil for the whole dish.
Kidney tip: chicken and rice provide phosphorus; keep to 90–100 g cooked chicken and avoid salty ready sauces. This dish is moderate in potassium.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 46 g carbohydrate; fill up on salad and vegetables and skip raisins and fried nuts on top.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Mandi), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Molokhia with Chicken
description: Saudi-style molokhia is cooked in chicken stock scented with mastic and cardamom, finished with a garlic and coriander fry and served with rice. This version uses skinless chicken breast, homemade stock instead of stock cubes, and only a little ghee and oil.
ingredients: 1 onion, quartered (100 g), 4 cardamom pods and 1 bay leaf
1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp cumin and ½ tsp black pepper
400 g fresh molokhia leaves, finely chopped (or frozen)
steps: Melt the ghee in a pot over medium heat, add the mastic and let it melt, then add the chicken and stir until it turns white.
Add the onion, cardamom, bay leaf, ground coriander, cumin, black pepper and 800 ml water, bring to the boil skimming the foam, then simmer for 20 minutes until the chicken is cooked.
Remove the onion pieces and bay leaf, add the molokhia and salt, stir well and let it come to the boil once or twice only, without a lid.
In a small pan heat the oil and cook the garlic until pale golden, then add the fresh coriander for a few seconds.
Stir the garlic fry into the molokhia, take off the heat and serve with lemon.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken breast, homemade stock with no stock cubes, and much less ghee and oil than the usual butter and ghee.
Kidney tip: molokhia is very high in potassium (about 1000 mg per bowl); keep to half a bowl, cut the molokhia to 250 g with more stock, and check with your dietitian before eating it.
Diabetes tip: the dish is low in carbohydrate (about 10 g); serve it with 150 g cooked rice, preferably basmati or brown.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Saudi Encyclopedia (ksaency), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Chicken Muqalqal
description: Chicken muqalqal is a quick Saudi dish in which chicken pieces are tossed on a saj with onion, tomato, bell pepper and spices. This version uses skinless chicken and a little olive oil, with no stock cubes and less salt.
serving_size: 1 plate (about 250 g), without rice or bread
ingredients: 300 g skinless chicken breast, cut in 3 cm cubes
250 g skinless, boneless chicken thighs, cubed
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp ground dried lime (loomi), ¼ tsp black pepper
steps: Heat the oil in a thick saj or wide pan over medium-high heat and stir the onion until soft and starting to brown.
Add the chicken and toss for 5 minutes until it changes colour on all sides, then add the garlic.
Add the tomatoes and spices and stir for 3 minutes, then the bell pepper, chilli and tomato paste.
Add the salt and 100 ml boiling water and stir, then cover and cook on medium-low heat for 15–20 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce thickens.
Uncover for the last 2 minutes to cook off extra liquid, sprinkle with coriander and serve hot with a green salad.
hints: What changed: no Maggi or stock cubes, skinless chicken, little oil, and no-salt-added tomato paste with about half the usual salt.

Kidney tip: chicken, tomatoes and tomato paste are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one plate (about 100 g cooked chicken), and you can leave out the tomato paste and halve the tomatoes. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: the nutrition values are for the muqalqal alone, without rice or bread; serve it with 150 g cooked rice (adds about 40 g carbohydrate) or one small whole-wheat bread and a large salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Mawdoo3 (chicken muqalqal), Al Bawaba News

title: Qatifi Khanfaroosh
description: Khanfaroosh is a traditional sweet of Qatif and Al-Ahsa, also known in Bahrain and across the Gulf: small rounds of flour, egg and sugar batter scented with cardamom, saffron and rose water, fried and served hot, especially in Ramadan. Here they are cooked in a non-stick pan with a little oil instead of fried, with less than half the sugar, low-fat milk, and no syrup.
ingredients: a pinch of saffron soaked in 2 tbsp rose water (30 ml)
1 tbsp olive or vegetable oil (15 g) for the pan
steps: Beat the eggs and sugar with an electric mixer until pale and fluffy.
Add the milk and saffron rose water, then both flours, milk powder, baking powder and cardamom, and beat until thick and creamy.
Cover and rest the batter for 10–15 minutes.
Heat a non-stick pan over low to medium heat and brush with a very thin layer of oil.
Drop one tablespoon of batter per round (or use a squeeze bottle), leaving space between them.
Cook until bubbles appear and the base is golden (1–2 minutes), then flip and cook 1 minute on the other side. Brush the pan again between batches (makes about 16 rounds).
Serve warm with tea or unsweetened Saudi coffee.
hints: What changed: 60 g sugar instead of about 200 g, cooked in a brushed pan instead of fried in oil, low-fat milk and nonfat milk powder, and no syrup poured over.
Kidney tip: milk and baking powder (which contains phosphate) add phosphorus; you can use water instead of milk and an extra spoon of flour instead of the milk powder, and keep to two rounds.
Diabetes tip: one serving has about 30 g carbohydrate, about 8 g of it added sugar; keep to two rounds with an unsweetened drink.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Mawdoo3, Al Jawhara Magazine

title: Chicken Kabsa
description: Chicken kabsa is Saudi Arabia's best-known rice dish, rooted in Najd: chicken simmered with onion, tomato and kabsa spices, then rice cooked in the same broth. This version uses skinless chicken, a homemade broth with no stock cubes or ready spice-salt mixes, one tablespoon of olive oil, a moderate rice portion and more vegetables.
ingredients: 600 g skinless, boneless chicken (thighs and breasts), cut into 8 pieces
2 tbsp tomato paste, no salt added (30 g)
1 green bell pepper, cut into strips (120 g)
2 tsp homemade salt-free kabsa spice (bezar), ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp turmeric
Whole spices: 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 2 bay leaves
15 g slivered almonds, dry-toasted, and fresh coriander to garnish
steps: Wash the rice until the water runs clear, soak it for 30 minutes, then drain.
Heat the oil in a wide pot, add the whole spices and onion and cook 5–6 minutes until soft and golden, then add the garlic for 1 minute.
Add the chicken and turn it for 5 minutes until it changes colour.
Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute, then add the grated tomato, carrot, kabsa spice, black pepper, turmeric and loomi and cook 5 minutes until thick.
Add the hot water and salt, cover and simmer 25–30 minutes until the chicken is cooked.
Lift the chicken onto a tray and brown it in an oven preheated to 220 °C for 10 minutes, with no added fat.

Measure the broth: you need about 375 ml for the rice; top up with water or boil to reduce. Add the drained rice, bell pepper and chilies and boil uncovered on high heat until the liquid drops to the level of the rice.
Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes, then turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes.
Fluff the rice with a fork, spread it on a serving platter, top with the chicken and garnish with almonds and coriander. Serve with green salad and homemade salt-free daqqus (tomato-chili sauce).
hints: What changed: no stock cubes or ready kabsa mix (the main source of salt in traditional kabsa), skinless chicken, one tablespoon of olive oil instead of butter, chicken browned in the oven instead of fried, and about 150 g cooked rice per person.

Kidney tip: tomatoes, tomato paste and almonds add potassium and phosphorus; on a low-potassium diet use 1 tbsp paste and skip the almonds. Keep to one plate and ask your dietitian about the right protein portion for you (before or on dialysis).
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 56 g carbohydrate; fill half your plate with salad, and you can swap half the rice for brown rice (add 100 ml more water and 10 minutes more cooking).
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Sayidaty Kitchen, Wikipedia (Kabsa)

title: Hail Muqashqash
description: Muqashqash is a traditional bread from the Hail region: a soft batter of whole wheat and laban left to turn slightly sour, dropped on a griddle, finished in the oven and soaked with honey and ghee. This version uses more whole-wheat flour, low-fat laban, and less than half the usual honey, ghee and baking powder.
ingredients: 1 tsp olive oil for wiping the griddle (4.5 g)
1 pinch each ground cardamom, cinnamon and dried lime (loomi)
steps: Mix both flours with the yeast, baking powder, sugar, salt and cardamom in a large bowl.
Whisk the egg with the laban, then add it to the flour little by little, mixing until you have a soft batter a little thicker than luqaimat batter.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 to 3 hours until puffed and slightly sour.
Heat the oven to 200 °C with the top element on. Heat a non-stick griddle over medium heat and wipe it with a little oil.
Drop coin-sized rounds of batter onto the griddle with a wet spoon and cook until the bottoms are golden.
Move the griddle to the oven for 5–7 minutes until the tops brown, then put the pieces in a covered container to stay soft. Repeat with the rest of the batter.
Warm the honey with the ghee and spices, pour it over the muqashqash, shake the container to coat, and serve warm.
hints: What changed: more than half the flour is whole wheat, the laban is low-fat, honey and ghee are less than half the traditional amount, and less baking powder keeps sodium down.
Kidney tip: laban, baking powder and whole-wheat flour contain phosphorus; keep to one portion (4 small pieces), and you can use low-sodium baking powder or rely on the yeast alone.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 29 g carbohydrate, including 7 g added sugar; serve the honey on the side and eat it with unsweetened laban or milk.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, M3aarf, Dlwaqty, Layalina Yummy

title: Hail-Style Lamb on Rice
description: Hail-style dhabiha is lamb cooked with turmeric, spices and red pepper, with the rice then cooked in its broth, and topped as in Hail homes with eggplant, boiled onions, an onion-raisin-loomi kashna and eggs. This is a scaled-down home version with about 600 g lean lamb instead of a whole animal, with less fat, no-salt tomato paste, limited salt and no stock cubes.
ingredients: 600 g lean lamb (shoulder or leg) in large pieces, visible fat trimmed (boneless weight)
1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp mixed spices (bezar), ½ tsp ground red pepper (Hail red pepper or paprika), 2 pierced dried limes (loomi), 4 cardamom pods
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
1 medium eggplant, cut in long wedges (250 g)
6 small onions, peeled and left whole (150 g)
1 tbsp white vinegar and ¼ tsp turmeric for boiling the vegetables
2 tsp ghee (9 g) and ½ tsp ground dried lime (loomi)
2 boiled eggs, halved (100 g), and lemon slices
steps: Rub the meat with the turmeric, mixed spices and red pepper, and put it in a wide pot with the onion, tomato, cardamom and loomi.
Pour the boiling water over the meat, skim the foam when it boils, then simmer for about 1½ hours until tender.
In a small pot boil the small onions and eggplant in water with the vinegar and turmeric for about 10 minutes until tender, then drain.
Strain the broth and skim the fat off the top; you need about 450 ml for the rice.
Heat the olive oil in the rice pot and cook the onion, tomato and tomato paste for 5 minutes, then add the broth and salt; when it boils add the drained rice.
Cook the rice on high heat until it absorbs most of the broth, then squeeze over the lemon, cover and cook on low heat for 15–20 minutes. Put the meat on top for the last 10 minutes to warm through.
For the kashna: heat the ghee in a frying pan and cook the sliced onion gently until soft and golden, then add the raisins and ground loomi for 2 minutes.
Spread the rice on a serving platter with the meat in the centre, arrange the eggplant, boiled onions, eggs and lemon slices around it, and spoon the kashna on top.
hints: What changed: a home batch with about 600 g meat instead of a whole lamb, trimmed meat with the fat skimmed off the broth, 2 tsp ghee instead of plenty of butter and oil, no-salt tomato paste instead of a can of regular paste, and no citric-salt seasoning or stock cubes.

Kidney tip: tomato, tomato paste, eggplant, raisins, meat and eggs provide potassium and phosphorus; keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked meat and 150 g cooked rice), and you can leave out the raisins and the half egg. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 60 g carbohydrate; take more of the eggplant and boiled onions, go easy on the raisins, and serve with a salad.
Suitable for: a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Mufattah), Mawdoo3 (Hail tamn)

title: Vegetable Kabsa
description: Vegetable kabsa is a popular home version of Saudi kabsa: mixed vegetables cooked with rice, kabsa spices and a little chicken, finished in a tray in the oven. Here the vegetables are roasted with a little olive oil instead of fried, there are more vegetables than rice, and no stock cubes.
ingredients: 2 medium carrots, sliced into rounds (150 g)
¼ head cauliflower, in florets (250 g)
1 green and 1 red bell pepper, sliced (200 g)
1 tbsp paprika, 1 tbsp salt-free kabsa spice (bezar), 2 pierced dried black limes
steps: Soak the potato slices in warm water for 2 hours (change the water once) to reduce potassium, then drain. Wash the rice and soak it for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 220 °C. Toss the potato, carrot, cauliflower, peppers and zucchini with 1 tbsp oil and half the paprika, spread in a tray and roast for 20 minutes, turning once.
Heat the teaspoon of oil in a non-stick pan and cook the chicken 6–8 minutes until cooked and golden, then remove. Soften the onion and garlic in the same pan with a splash of water.
Boil the rice in plenty of unsalted water for 8 minutes until half-cooked, then drain.
In a deep ovenproof dish layer the onion and garlic, then the roasted vegetables and chicken, then the rice on top.
Bring the blended tomato, water, spices, remaining paprika, loomi and salt to the boil and pour over the rice.
Cover with foil and bake at 200 °C for 25 minutes until the rice is tender and has absorbed the liquid.
Turn out onto a platter or serve straight from the dish, with green salad.
hints: What changed: the vegetables are roasted with one tablespoon of oil instead of fried in lots of oil, the chicken is skinless breast in a moderate amount, there is less rice and more vegetables, and no stock cubes.
Kidney tip: potato, tomato and cauliflower are high in potassium; soak the potato as in the first step or replace it with extra zucchini and pepper, and keep to one plate.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 68 g carbohydrate, part of it from the potato; you can leave out the potato to cut starch, and mix in half brown rice.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Sayidaty Kitchen, Hia Magazine

title: Hasawi Rice with Chicken
description: Hasawi rice is a popular dish from Al-Ahsa in the Eastern Province: the local red Hasawi rice is cooked in a spiced chicken broth, topped with oven-browned chicken and an onion-raisin topping, and smoked with charcoal. This version uses skinless chicken and homemade broth without stock cubes, with less oil, ghee, salt and raisins, and dry-toasted instead of fried nuts.
ingredients: 600 g skinless chicken (300 g thighs and 300 g breast), in large pieces
1 medium tomato (120 g) and 1 small carrot (80 g)
Whole spices: 5 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, ½ tsp black peppercorns, 1 cinnamon stick, 2 pierced dried limes (loomi), 2 grains mastic
1 tsp mixed spice (bezar) and ½ tsp turmeric to rub on the chicken
200 g red Hasawi rice (or brown long-grain rice)
1 tbsp no-salt-added tomato paste (15 g) and 2 garlic cloves, crushed (10 g)
¾ tsp salt (4 g) for the whole pot
½ tsp curry powder, ½ tsp ground dried lime, a pinch each of cardamom and cinnamon
1 tsp ghee (4.5 g) and 1 small piece of charcoal for smoking
steps: Wash the Hasawi rice and soak it in warm water for 1 hour.
Put the chicken in a pot with the quartered onion, tomato, carrot, whole spices and water. Bring to the boil, lower the heat, skim, and simmer 30–35 minutes until cooked.
Lift out the chicken, rub it with the bezar, turmeric and a little broth, and brown it in a 220 °C oven for 15–20 minutes.
Strain the broth and keep about 700 ml; mash the tomato and carrot into it if you like.

Return the broth to the pot with the tomato paste and garlic, add the drained rice and the salt, bring to the boil, then cover and cook on low heat 35–40 minutes until the red rice is tender and has absorbed the broth; add a little hot water if needed.

For the topping: warm the olive oil in a pan and cook the sliced onion, covered, on low heat for 15 minutes until soft and golden; add the curry, dried lime, cardamom, cinnamon and raisins and stir for 2 minutes.
Lay the browned chicken on the rice, set a small heatproof bowl with the ghee in the middle of the pot, drop the hot charcoal into it, close the lid at once and leave 10 minutes.
Remove the bowl and charcoal, spoon the rice onto a platter, top with the chicken and onion topping, sprinkle with the almonds, and serve with a green salad and daqoos.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken, homemade broth without stock cubes, 1 tbsp oil instead of about 80 ml, ghee only for smoking, fewer raisins, dry-toasted almonds instead of fried nuts, and under ¼ tsp salt per serving.
Kidney tip: red rice, almonds, raisins and tomato paste add potassium and phosphorus; you can swap half the red rice for white basmati, cut or skip the raisins and almonds, and keep to one serving.
Diabetes tip: one serving has about 150 g cooked rice; red Hasawi rice is high in fibre, so serve it with a large salad and go light on the raisins.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3, Hia Magazine, Dawan

title: Najdi Marasee with Onion Broth
description: Marasee is a Najdi dish from Al-Qassim: thin rounds of whole-wheat dough pressed out by hand, cooked on a saj griddle, then moistened with an onion and dried-lime broth (balool) or eaten with honey. This is the savoury dough version; the broth is made with olive oil and a little ghee, tomato and zucchini, with no sugar, no bouillon and little salt.
ingredients: 1 tsp oil (4.5 g) for the hands and griddle
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) and 1 tsp ghee (4.5 g)
Spices: 1 tsp ground dried lime, 3 crushed cardamom pods, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp mixed spices, black pepper
Salt: ¾ tsp (4 g) in total: a quarter in the dough, the rest in the broth
steps: Mix the flour, yeast and a quarter of the salt, add the warm water gradually and knead to a very soft, slightly sticky dough; cover and rest for 1 hour.
Divide the dough into 16 walnut-sized balls and oil your hands lightly.

Heat a saj or non-stick pan over medium heat, press each ball with your palm straight onto the hot surface into a thin round, cook 1 minute, then flip until browned in spots. Keep the marasee covered.
For the balool: heat the oil and ghee and cook the onion until soft and golden, then add the cardamom, dried lime, turmeric and spices for 1 minute.
Add the tomato and zucchini and stir 5 minutes, then pour in the boiling water and the remaining salt and simmer 10 minutes.
Tear the marasee into pieces in a deep dish, pour the hot balool over, leave 2 minutes to soak in, and serve at once with low-fat laban or a salad.
hints: What changed: no sugar in the broth, olive oil with one teaspoon of ghee instead of plenty of butter, no bouillon, and tomato and zucchini for more vegetables.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour is higher in phosphorus and potassium than white flour; you can use half and half and less tomato, and keep to one plate. Ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 51 g carbohydrate with 8 g fibre; add a protein such as a boiled egg or some grilled chicken, and skip the honey.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Marasee), Mawdoo3 (marasee), Qassimy.com (marasee recipes)

title: Fish Mandi
description: Fish mandi, popular in Saudi coastal cities, is a dish in which grouper stuffed with onion, tomato and coriander cooks above spiced rice so its juices flavour the rice. We cut the oil and salt and left out the stock cubes; grouper is naturally lean.
ingredients: 600 g grouper (thick steaks or a whole fish split along the belly)
1 tsp mixed spices, ½ tsp turmeric, ¼ tsp salt
A small bunch of fresh coriander, chopped (20 g)
200 g basmati rice, washed and drained
1 green chilli (15 g), 1 dried lime, 4 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, ½ tsp cumin
steps: Rinse and dry the fish, rub it with the lemon juice, spices, turmeric and ¼ tsp salt and leave 20 minutes.
For the stuffing: cook the onion and garlic in the teaspoon of oil for 3 minutes, then add the tomato, coriander and vinegar and cook 2 minutes until thick.
Fill the fish with the stuffing (or spread it between the steaks) and close it.
Heat the oven to 200°C. In a pot, soften the rice onion in the oil, add the spices, chilli, salt and water; when hot add the rice, stir and pour into an oven tray.
Cover the tray with pierced foil, lay the fish on top and cover it with more foil.
Bake 40–45 minutes until the rice is tender and the fish flakes easily, then uncover the fish and brown it under the grill for 5 minutes.
Optionally smoke it with a piece of charcoal for 3 minutes, then serve with lemon wedges and salad.
hints: What changed: the fish is baked, not fried, less than 2 tbsp oil for the whole dish, no stock cubes and much less salt.
Kidney tip: grouper is rich in potassium and phosphorus; keep to 100–120 g cooked fish and use less tomato in the stuffing if you must limit potassium.
Diabetes and heart tip: fish is a lean, heart-friendly protein; one plate has about 48 g carbohydrate, so add plenty of salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen, Elbalad News (fish mandi)

title: Hijazi Mabshoor
description: Mabshoor is a Makkah dish of spiced minced-meat balls cooked on a griddle and served with garlic yoghurt, a red tomato sauce and white rice. We used lean minced lamb leg, far less oil, low-fat yoghurt and little salt.
ingredients: 1 small onion, grated and squeezed (100 g)
1 tsp grill spice mix, 1 tsp paprika, ½ tsp black pepper
2 tsp olive oil (9 g): one for the mix, one for the griddle
1 small onion (100 g) and 2 garlic cloves (8 g)
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
1 tsp olive oil (4.5 g), 5 cardamom pods, ¼ tsp salt (1.5 g)
steps: Mix the meat with the grated onion, spices, 1 tsp oil and the salt, knead well, cover and chill for at least 1 hour.
For the garlic yoghurt: stir the crushed garlic into the yoghurt and keep it in the fridge.
For the sauce: blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic, then simmer with the oil, paprika and salt over low heat for 10–15 minutes until thick.
For the rice: bring 400 ml water to the boil with the cardamom, oil and salt, add the drained rice, cover and cook on low heat for 15 minutes.

Shape the meat into walnut-sized balls, brush a griddle or iron pan with the remaining teaspoon of oil and cook the balls over medium-low heat, turning, until the juices dry and they are cooked through (8–10 minutes), or grill them over charcoal.
Serve the Makkah way in three parts: on the garlic yoghurt, in the red sauce and over the rice, with a green salad.
hints: What changed: lean minced leg meat instead of meat with added fat, 2 tbsp oil for the whole dish instead of about 250 ml of oils, low-fat yoghurt and much less salt.
Kidney tip: yoghurt, tomato and meat are high in phosphorus and potassium; halve the yoghurt, keep the sauce to 2 tbsp per person and stick to one portion of meat (about 90 g cooked).
Diabetes tip: the plate has about 57 g carbohydrate, mostly from the rice; you can serve the mabshoor with the yoghurt and salad and halve the rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen, Elwasfa

title: Tangy Stuffed Grape Leaves
description: Saudi-style tangy stuffed grape leaves: vine leaves filled with rice, tomato, onion and herbs, slowly cooked in a sauce of lemon, pomegranate molasses and olive oil. This version uses fresh or frozen leaves instead of salty brined ones, far less oil, and no sugar or stock cubes.
ingredients: 250 g fresh or frozen grape leaves (about 50 leaves), blanched 1 minute
240 g short-grain (Egyptian) rice, washed, soaked 30 minutes and drained
30 g parsley, 20 g coriander, 10 g mint and 10 g dill, all chopped
1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp mixed spice
1 small onion in rings (50 g) and 1 tomato in slices (100 g) to line the pot
steps: Soften the onion, garlic and chilli in the tablespoon of oil, then add the chopped tomatoes and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the rice and spices and stir for 3 minutes, then turn off the heat, add the herbs and mix well.
Line the bottom of the pot with the onion rings, tomato slices and a few grape leaves.
Lay each leaf shiny side down, put a heaped tablespoon of filling on it, fold in the sides and roll tightly, then pack the rolls close together in the pot.
Mix the cooking-liquid ingredients, pour over the rolls to cover them, and weigh them down with an upside-down plate.
Cook on high heat for 10 minutes, then on very low heat for 1½ to 2 hours until the rice and leaves are tender.
Leave it in the pot to cool completely, then turn it out onto a serving plate and garnish with pomegranate seeds.
hints: What changed: fresh or frozen leaves instead of brined ones (brined leaves are very salty; if you use them, soak in hot water, change the water twice and add no salt), 2 tbsp oil instead of a large amount, and no sugar or stock cubes.
Kidney tip: grape leaves are rich in calcium with moderate potassium, and tomato and herbs add more potassium; keep to 8 rolls and you can use less tomato in the cooking liquid.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 49 g carbohydrate from the rice; serve it with low-fat laban or salad and have it instead of rice in that meal, not as well as rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Cookpad

title: Liver (Kabda)
description: Kabda is a popular Saudi breakfast dish, best known in the Hijaz: lamb liver seared fast on a hot pan with onion, peppers and tomato and finished with lemon and coriander. This version uses a little olive oil instead of suet, leaves out the heart and kidneys, and uses less salt, added at the end.
ingredients: 500 g fresh lamb liver, cut into long thin strips
steps: Rinse the liver, remove the membranes and veins, pat it dry and cut it into long thin strips.
Heat the oil in a wide pan or saj over high heat. Add the bay leaves, chilli and onion and stir until the onion softens and starts to brown, then add the garlic for half a minute.
Add the liver in two batches so the pan stays hot, and stir for 3–4 minutes until browned on all sides.
Sprinkle in the cumin, dried coriander, turmeric and black pepper and stir.
Add the tomato and then the bell pepper, stir for 2 minutes, then cover for 2 minutes over medium heat so the liver stays moist in the tomato juices. Do not overcook or it will dry out.
Turn off the heat, add the salt, lemon juice and fresh coriander, stir and serve hot straight away.
hints: What changed: no suet, heart or kidneys, only 2 tbsp olive oil for four people, and a small amount of salt added at the end, with lemon and spices for flavour.
Heart tip: liver is very high in cholesterol (about 460 mg per serving), so people with heart disease or high cholesterol should eat it once a week or less; half a portion is enough.
Kidney tip: liver is high in phosphorus and protein, and tomato and peppers add potassium; keep to half a portion (about 60 g cooked liver), use one tomato only and more onion and bell pepper.
Diabetes tip: the dish itself is low in carbohydrate; serve it with a quarter of a wholewheat flatbread (about 30 g) and a green salad instead of white bread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, House of Saud (Saudi breakfast guide), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Hasawi Madrouba (Saliqiya)
description: Hasawi madrouba, also called saliqiya, is a dish from Al-Ahsa in the Eastern Province: rice cooked with chicken or meat, mung beans and Swiss chard (silq), then beaten until smooth. This version uses skinless chicken breast, olive oil with a little ghee instead of a lot of butter, fewer mung beans, no stock cubes and little salt.
ingredients: 500 g skinless chicken breast, in medium pieces
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
40 g mung beans, soaked 4 hours, then boiled 15 minutes and drained
250 g Swiss chard leaves (1 large bunch), chopped
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) and 2 tsp ghee (9 g)
Spices: 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp mixed spices, 1 tsp ground dried lime, 1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp ground ginger, a pinch of cinnamon and black pepper
A handful of chopped parsley (20 g) and of fresh coriander (15 g)
steps: Heat the oil and ghee in a pot and cook the onion 5 minutes until golden, then add the garlic, tomato, tomato paste, spices and half the parsley and coriander and stir for 5 minutes.
Add the chicken and turn it in the sauce, then pour in the boiling water and simmer 25 minutes until cooked.
Meanwhile blanch the chard in boiling water for 3 minutes, drain and discard the water.
Add the drained rice, cooked mung beans and salt, cover and cook 15 minutes on medium heat then 20 minutes on low until the rice is very soft; add a little boiling water if it dries.
Stir in the chard until wilted, then beat the mixture with a wooden masher or potato masher until smooth, leaving a little of the chicken in shreds.
Add the lemon juice and the rest of the parsley and coriander and serve hot with a cucumber salad.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes, olive oil and a little ghee instead of 60 g butter, skinless chicken, and no fried onion garnish.

Kidney tip: chard and mung beans are very high in potassium and phosphorus; blanching the chard and soaking and boiling the mung beans, then discarding the water, lowers the potassium, and you can halve the chard. Keep to one plate and ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 56 g carbohydrate; the mung beans and chard add fibre that slows sugar absorption, and you can swap a quarter of the rice for soaked brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Hia Magazine, Cookpad Saudi Arabia (Hasawi madrouba)

title: Hasawi Hareesa
description: Hasawi hareesa is a favourite dish of Al-Ahsa in Ramadan and at Eid: wheat cooked for hours with chicken or meat and just water until it melts, then beaten and served white with a well of ghee in the centre. This version uses skinless chicken, about a teaspoon of ghee per serving instead of plenty of ghee, and little salt.
ingredients: 240 g hareis wheat (Hasawi red wheat if available), washed and soaked at least 2 hours
1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 1 small whole onion (70 g)
A pinch of ground cinnamon to serve (optional)
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with water to cover, boil for 5 minutes, then discard the water and foam.
Return the chicken to the pot with the drained wheat, cinnamon, cardamom, onion and water; the water should be about 3 cm above the grain.

Bring to the boil, then cover and cook on very low heat for 4–5 hours, stirring now and then and adding hot water when needed, until the grains burst and the chicken falls apart (or 1½ hours in a pressure cooker).
Remove the cinnamon, cardamom and onion, add the salt and beat at once while hot with a wooden masher or hand blender until smooth and stretchy; add hot water if it is too thick.
Spread it in bowls, make a small well in the centre, add about a teaspoon of melted ghee to each, and dust with a little cinnamon if you like.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken boiled first to remove fat, about a teaspoon of ghee per bowl instead of pouring plenty, and less salt with flavour from cinnamon and cardamom.
Kidney tip: whole wheat and chicken are high in phosphorus and protein; keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked chicken) or smaller as your dietitian advises.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 44 g carbohydrate from whole grain; do not sprinkle sugar on top as some people do, and serve with a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Al-Madina newspaper (hareis on the Hasawi Ramadan table), Cookpad (Hasawi hareesa)

title: Fish Kabsa
description: Fish kabsa is a dish of Saudi Arabia's coasts and the Gulf: rice cooked with onion, tomato and spices, served with spiced fish. In this version the fish is baked instead of fried, and the rice uses little oil and a homemade broth with no stock cubes.
ingredients: 600 g hamour (grouper) or kingfish fillet, cut into 4 pieces
1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp ground coriander, ½ tsp turmeric, ¼ tsp black pepper
2 medium tomatoes, peeled and chopped (240 g)
2 tbsp tomato paste, no salt added (30 g)
2 pierced dried black limes, 1½ tsp salt-free kabsa spice (bezar), and a pinch of saffron soaked in 2 tbsp water
Whole spices: 1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves
¾ tsp salt (4.5 g), a pinch of it for the fish
steps: Mix the lemon juice, garlic, cumin, coriander, turmeric, black pepper and the pinch of salt; coat the fish and chill for 20 minutes.
Wash the rice, soak it for 30 minutes, then drain.
Heat the oil in a pot, add the whole spices and onion and cook until golden, then the garlic for 1 minute.
Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute, then the tomatoes, half the coriander, chilies, loomi and kabsa spice, and cook 5 minutes until thick.
Add the hot water and the rest of the salt and simmer 10 minutes, then add the rice and boil on high heat until the liquid drops to the level of the rice.
Sprinkle the saffron over the rice, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile place the fish in a tray brushed with the teaspoon of oil and bake in an oven preheated to 200 °C for 12–15 minutes until it flakes easily.
Spread the rice on a platter, top with the fish, sprinkle with the remaining coriander and serve with lemon wedges and green salad.
hints: What changed: the fish is baked instead of fried, the rice is cooked with one tablespoon of oil instead of butter, and there are no stock cubes or salted spice mixes.
Kidney tip: fish, tomatoes and tomato paste add potassium and phosphorus; keep to one piece of fish (about 110 g cooked), and cut the paste to 1 tbsp on a low-potassium diet.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 52 g carbohydrate; serve with a large green salad, and you can mix in half brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), WebTeb, Elbalad

title: Hijazi Aysh Bil-Lahm (Meat Bread)
description: Aysh bil-lahm (aysh abu al-lahm) is one of the best-known dishes of Makkah and the Hijaz: a yeast dough flavoured with nigella and fennel is spread in a tray and covered with minced meat cooked with leeks and a tahini and vinegar sauce, then topped with tomato and sesame and baked. Here half the flour is whole wheat, the mince is lean, tahini and oil are cut well down, and salt is limited with no stock cubes.
serving_size: a quarter of the tray (about 320 g)
ingredients: 1 tsp nigella seeds + ½ tsp crushed fennel seeds
1 tbsp olive oil (15 ml) for the dough + 1 tsp (5 ml) for the tray
1 tsp cumin + ¼ tsp black pepper
1 egg (50 g), beaten, for the top
steps: Mix both flours with the yeast, sugar, salt, nigella and fennel, then add the dough oil and the warm water little by little and knead for 8–10 minutes until soft and elastic. Cover and leave to rise for 45 minutes.

Cook the onion and minced beef in a non-stick pan without oil over medium heat, breaking up the meat with a spoon, until the liquid has evaporated and the meat has changed colour, about 10 minutes. Add the cumin, black pepper and the filling salt.
Whisk the tahini with the vinegar, water and garlic to a creamy sauce, then mix it with the cooked meat and the chopped leeks.
Heat the oven to 200 °C and oil a 30 cm round tray with the tray oil.
Press the dough into the tray, raising the edges a little, and spread the meat mixture over it, leaving a 2 cm border.
Fold the border slightly over the filling and brush it with beaten egg, pour the rest of the egg over the filling, then lay the tomato slices on top and sprinkle with sesame.
Rest the tray for 10 minutes, then bake on the middle shelf for 25–30 minutes until the base and edges are browned, browning the top for the last 2 minutes.
Leave for 5 minutes, cut into four and serve with a green salad or rocket.
hints: What changed: half the flour is whole wheat, 5%-fat mince cooked without oil, 40 g tahini instead of ¾ of a glass, only 20 ml oil instead of half a glass in the dough, and 4 g salt for the whole tray instead of plenty of salt and a stock cube.

Kidney tip: meat, tahini and whole-wheat flour are sources of phosphorus, and tomato and leeks contain potassium; you can use all white flour and cut the meat to 350 g with more leeks, and keep to a quarter of the tray.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 70 g carbohydrate; cut the tray into six pieces instead and have one piece with a large plate of salad.
Best kept as an occasional dish for kidney, diabetes and heart diets; keep to one serving.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Maw9i3i

title: Sweet Vermicelli
description: Sweet vermicelli is a common Saudi and Gulf breakfast and Eid dish: vermicelli toasted in ghee, then cooked with water and sugar, cardamom and saffron. Here the ghee and sugar are cut to less than half, there is no salt, and cardamom, saffron and rose water carry the flavour.
ingredients: a pinch of saffron soaked in 1 tbsp rose water
steps: Melt the ghee in a wide pot over medium heat, add the broken vermicelli and stir constantly for 4–5 minutes until evenly golden but not dark.
Add the sugar and cardamom and stir for 1 minute.
Add the hot water and the saffron in rose water and stir, then cover, lower the heat and cook for 8–10 minutes until the water is absorbed and the vermicelli is tender.
Fluff with a fork to separate the strands and serve warm.
hints: What changed: less ghee and less than half the usual sugar, no salt, and flavour from cardamom, saffron and rose water.
Kidney tip: this dish is relatively low in potassium, sodium and phosphorus, so it is a suitable sweet in one portion; avoid adding nuts or milk.

Diabetes tip: one portion has about 47 g carbohydrate; have half a portion with a boiled egg or a vegetable omelette (balaleet style) to slow the rise in blood sugar, and choose whole-wheat vermicelli.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Cookpad Saudi Arabia, WebTeb

title: Hijazi Kabli Rice with Lamb
description: Kabli is a rice dish that came from Kabul and became a well-known feast dish of the Hijaz (Makkah, Jeddah and Madinah): lamb cooked with cumin-scented basmati rice and topped with caramelised carrots, raisins and almonds. This version uses lean leg of lamb, much less oil and sugar, and more carrots.
ingredients: 550 g boneless lean leg of lamb, trimmed, cut into medium pieces
4 cardamom pods, 3 cloves, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked for 30 minutes
3 carrots (300 g), cut into thin sticks
1 tbsp lemon juice (15 ml) and lemon wedges
steps: Put the lamb in a pot with the onion, garlic, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, bay leaf, black pepper and water. Bring to the boil, skim, then cover and simmer for 60–75 minutes until tender.
Lift out the lamb and keep it covered. Strain the broth and measure 400 ml for the rice (top up with water if needed).

In a frying pan, heat 1 tbsp of the oil, toast the almonds for a minute and lift them out. Add the carrots and stir for 5 minutes, sprinkle in the sugar and stir until glossy and lightly caramelised, add 3 tbsp water and cover for 5 minutes until tender, then add the raisins for a minute.

In the pot, heat the rest of the oil and toast the cumin seeds for half a minute. Add the measured broth and the salt; when it boils add the drained rice and cook over high heat until most of the liquid is absorbed.
Arrange the lamb and half of the carrots on the rice, cover tightly (you can wrap the lid in a cloth) and leave on very low heat for 20–25 minutes.
