Spoon the rice and lamb onto a platter, top with the remaining carrots, raisins and almonds, sprinkle with lemon juice and serve with lemon wedges and a green salad.
hints: What changed: 2 tbsp oil instead of the large amount used in traditional recipes, only 10 g sugar for the carrots instead of a heavy caramel, trimmed leg of lamb, 150 g cooked rice per portion with more carrots, and no stock cubes.

Kidney tip: raisins, almonds, carrots and meat add potassium and phosphorus; cut the raisins to 20 g and the almonds to 10 g, keep to about 60–90 g cooked meat per portion, and boil and drain the carrots before glazing them.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 63 g carbohydrate; keep to 150 g cooked rice, you can make half of it brown rice, and start the meal with a large salad.
Suitable for: a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Layalina Yummy, Duyoufi Foods

title: Hijazi Saqdana (Sago Pudding)
description: Saqdana is a chilled Makkah dessert of sago pearls cooked in milk with cardamom, much loved in Ramadan after the pre-dawn meal. We used low-fat milk, less than a third of the usual sugar and small portions.
steps: Put the sago and hot water in a pot over low heat and stir constantly until the pearls turn from white to almost clear (about 10 minutes).
Add the milk gradually, raise the heat to medium and keep stirring for 10 minutes until the mixture thickens.
Add the sugar and cardamom and stir over low heat for 5 minutes, then turn off the heat and add the rose water.
Divide between 6 small glasses or bowls, cover and let cool, then chill for 4 hours.
hints: What changed: low-fat milk instead of full-cream milk powder, and 60 g sugar instead of about 200 g, in small portions.
Kidney tip: milk is a source of phosphorus and potassium; keep to one small glass, and you can replace a third of the milk with water or a plant milk without added phosphate.
Diabetes tip: one glass has about 31 g carbohydrate including 10 g added sugar; eat it after a meal rather than on its own, or use a sugar substitute.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen, Cookpad

title: Desert Truffles (Faqa) with Onion
description: Faqa (desert truffle) is a seasonal desert fungus gathered in winter and spring in Saudi Arabia and traditionally cooked slowly with onion and peppers, then served with rice or bread. This version uses olive oil instead of butter, no stock cubes or seasoning powder, and little salt.
ingredients: 600 g desert truffles (faqa), cleaned and peeled
1 small green bell pepper (100 g), chopped
1 small handful fresh coriander (10 g), chopped
steps: Soak the truffles in water for an hour, then scrub them one by one, scrape off the thin skin with a knife, peel the base where the sand collects, and rinse several times until no sand is left.
Cut the truffles into medium cubes.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and soften the onion without browning it. Add the garlic, then the bell pepper and chilli, and stir for a minute.
Add the truffles, bezar, turmeric and black pepper and stir well. Lower the heat, cover and cook for 30 minutes, stirring now and then; the truffles will release their water.
Uncover and raise the heat a little for the last 10 minutes until the liquid evaporates and the truffles brown slightly, then add the salt.
Sprinkle with fresh coriander and serve with rice or wholewheat bread.
hints: What changed: olive oil instead of butter and ghee, no seasoning powder or stock cubes, and only ½ tsp salt for four people. The nutrition is calculated using white mushrooms as an approximate stand-in for faqa.

Kidney tip: truffles and mushrooms are high in potassium; keep to half a portion (about 150 g truffles) with more onion and bell pepper, and you can boil the cut truffles for 10 minutes and drain them before cooking to lower the potassium.
Diabetes tip: the dish is low in carbohydrate; serve it with 150 g cooked rice (basmati, or half brown) or a quarter of a wholewheat flatbread, with a salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3, Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Najdi Fareek with Dates and Onion
description: Fareek (mafrooka) is a winter dish from Najd and Qassim: a thick whole-wheat loaf baked in embers or the oven, then crumbled and rubbed with ghee and dates or onion. This version uses only a little ghee with olive oil and sweetens with dates instead of sugar, with no added sugar.
ingredients: ½ tsp ground ginger and 1 tsp ground cinnamon
½ tsp ground cinnamon and ½ tsp ground dried lime (loomi)
steps: Mix the flour with the milk powder, yeast, salt, ginger and cinnamon, add the water gradually and knead a soft, firm dough.
Oil a sheet of foil with 1 tsp of the oil, shape the dough on it into a thick round (about 3 cm), wrap it up and leave 30 minutes.
Bake at 180 °C for 50–60 minutes until cooked through, then open the foil and leave 10 more minutes to brown.
Cook the onion in the rest of the oil over medium heat until soft and golden, then add the cinnamon and dried lime.
Crumble the hot loaf coarsely by hand or in a food processor, removing any hard edges.
Rub the crumbs with the warm ghee and chopped dates until evenly mixed, then fold in the onion and serve warm with lemon.
hints: What changed: much less ghee than usual with a little olive oil, dates for sweetness instead of icing sugar or honey, and a whole-wheat loaf.
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour and dates are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to one small bowl, and you can swap a third of the whole-wheat flour for white flour and use fewer dates.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 48 g carbohydrate, including the sugar from the dates; eat it with laban or unsweetened Arabic coffee and stop at one bowl.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, WebTeb, Cookpad

title: Shrimp Jareesh
description: Shrimp jareesh is a Gulf-style home dish also cooked in Saudi Arabia, in which cracked wheat (jareesh) cooks in an onion-tomato sauce with shrimp, dried lime and turmeric. This version uses a moderate amount of shrimp, a little olive oil, no stock cubes, less salt and more vegetables.
ingredients: 200 g jareesh (cracked wheat), lightly toasted in a dry pan, then washed and soaked 30 minutes
Spices: 1 cinnamon stick, 2 pierced dried limes (loomi), ½ tsp turmeric, 1 tsp curry powder, ½ tsp ground cardamom, ½ tsp ground dried lime
1 small bunch fresh coriander, chopped (30 g)
steps: Heat the oil in a pot and cook the onion until soft and lightly golden, then add the garlic, ginger, cinnamon stick and whole dried limes for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes, tomato paste, turmeric, curry powder, cardamom and ground dried lime, and stir for 5 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Add the shrimp and stir for 2 minutes until coated and just pink, then lift it out onto a plate.
Pour in the boiling water, add the bell pepper, chilli and half the coriander, and bring to the boil.
Add the drained jareesh and the salt, cover and simmer on low heat for 35–40 minutes, stirring now and then, until the grains are swollen and tender; add a little boiling water if it dries out.
Return the shrimp with the lemon juice and simmer just 5 minutes more so it stays tender.
Garnish with the rest of the coriander and serve with a green salad and cucumber.
hints: What changed: about half the usual shrimp, no stock cubes, olive oil instead of a ghee or fat topping, less salt and extra bell pepper.
Kidney tip: jareesh (a whole grain), shrimp, tomatoes and tomato paste are rich in phosphorus and potassium; keep to one plate and you can halve the tomatoes. Ask your dietitian about your portion.

Diabetes and heart tip: one plate has about 49 g carbohydrate with plenty of fibre from the jareesh; start with the salad. Shrimp is high in cholesterol, so keep to this portion and do not have it every day.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Zahrat Al Khaleej, Maggi Arabia (jareesh with prawns)

title: Hijazi Saleeq with Lamb
description: Saleeq is a Hijazi dish famous in Taif: rice simmered for a long time in meat broth and then milk until creamy, served with browned meat. This version uses lean lamb, low-fat milk, only two teaspoons of ghee instead of the usual large amount, and little salt with no stock cubes.
ingredients: 560 g lean lamb leg, visible fat trimmed, in large pieces
Whole spices: 5 cardamom pods, 2 bay leaves, 1 cinnamon stick, 2 mastic grains
200 g short-grain (Egyptian) rice, washed and soaked 1 hour
2 tsp ghee (9 g) with 2 mastic grains, to serve
1 tsp olive oil (4.5 g) with ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp mixed spices and black pepper, to brush the lamb
Salt: 1 scant tsp (5 g) for the whole pot
1 tomato (150 g), a handful of coriander (15 g), 1 green chilli (10 g), 1 tbsp lemon juice (15 ml), 1 small garlic clove (3 g), 60 ml cold water
steps: Put the lamb in a pot with the water, bring to the boil and skim off the foam.
Add the onion and whole spices and simmer 1 to 1½ hours until the lamb is tender, then lift it out and strain the broth.
Measure about 1 l of broth back into the pot, add the drained rice and half the salt and simmer 30–40 minutes without much stirring until the rice is very soft; add a little broth if it dries.
Add the hot milk little by little, stirring and beating the rice with a wooden spoon until creamy and smooth, then leave 10 minutes on very low heat.
Brush the lamb with the oil, turmeric, spices and remaining salt and brown it under the oven grill at 220°C for 10–15 minutes.
Blend the dagoos ingredients and serve chilled.
Warm the ghee with the mastic for a few seconds, pour it over the saleeq in the serving dish, top with the lamb and serve at once with the dagoos and a green salad.
hints: What changed: lean, trimmed lamb, low-fat milk instead of full-fat or powdered milk, very little ghee, no bouillon and much less salt; the flavour comes from cardamom and mastic.
Kidney tip: milk and meat are high in phosphorus and tomato in potassium; keep to one portion (90–100 g cooked meat), and you can swap half the milk for broth. Ask your dietitian.
Diabetes tip: long-cooked soft rice raises blood sugar quickly; one plate has about 51 g carbohydrate, so do not go beyond it and start with the salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Arabic Wikipedia (Saleeq Taifi), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Hijazi Halawa Labaniya
description: Labaniya is a soft Hijazi milk sweet popular in Makkah and Madinah, made from milk powder, sugar syrup, ghee and cardamom and cut into squares. This version uses skimmed milk powder with a little ghee, cuts the sugar to less than half the usual amount, and keeps the pieces small.
steps: Brush a small tray (20 × 15 cm) very lightly with ghee or line it with baking paper.
Put the sugar and water in a small pot and stir until the sugar dissolves, then boil over high heat for 5–6 minutes without stirring until the syrup thickens slightly.
Turn off the heat and stir in the ghee, cardamom and rose water.

Add half the milk powder and stir quickly with a wooden spoon, then add the rest and keep stirring until a soft, cohesive dough forms. (If it stays too soft, return it to low heat for a minute while stirring.)
Press the dough into the tray 1.5 cm thick, sprinkle the pistachios on top and press them in lightly.
Let it cool completely, then chill for 2 hours and cut into 12 pieces.
hints: What changed: skimmed instead of full-cream milk powder, less than half the usual sugar, and a little ghee; it stays soft like traditional labaniya but is less sweet.
Kidney tip: milk powder is very high in phosphorus and potassium; have one piece on special occasions only, and on dialysis take it with your phosphate binder as your doctor advises.
Diabetes tip: one piece has about 15 g carbohydrate (6 g of it added sugar); stick to one piece with Arabic coffee and no other sweets.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia, WebTeb

title: Hijazi Sahlab
description: Hijazi sahlab is a winter drink from Makkah, Jeddah and Madinah: milk cooked with ginger water and cardamom, thickened with ground rice, scented with rose water and topped with almonds. This version uses low-fat milk instead of full-fat milk powder, half the usual sugar and fewer almonds.
ingredients: ½ tsp ground cardamom (1 g) + ½ tsp to garnish
50 g rice flour (finely ground Egyptian rice)
30 g blanched almonds, half ground and half chopped
a pinch of ground cinnamon or ginger to garnish
steps: Boil the water with the grated ginger and cardamom over medium heat for 15–20 minutes, then strain and keep the ginger water.
In another pan whisk the cold milk with the rice flour and sugar until there are no lumps.
Add the ginger water and cook over low heat, stirring all the time, until it boils and starts to thicken, about 8–10 minutes.
Add the ground almonds and rose water and stir for 2 more minutes until creamy.
Pour into warm mugs, top with the chopped almonds and a pinch of cinnamon or ginger and serve hot.
hints: What changed: liquid low-fat milk instead of full-fat milk powder, 40 g sugar instead of about 100 g, and 30 g almonds instead of about 140 g.
If you can get pure salep powder (orchid root) from a spice seller, use 1 tbsp of it instead of the rice flour and sprinkle it slowly over the hot milk while whisking so it does not form lumps.
Kidney tip: milk and almonds are sources of phosphorus and potassium; you can replace half the milk with water or a plant milk without added phosphate, and keep to half a mug.
Diabetes tip: one mug has about 22 g carbohydrate; cut the sugar to 1 tbsp or use a zero-calorie sweetener, and drink it with a meal rather than on its own.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Sahha wa Hana

title: Lentil Soup
description: Saudi-style lentil soup is cooked with a base of onion, garlic, peppers and spices plus vegetables such as pumpkin and carrot, then blended smooth; it is a Ramadan and winter favourite. This version uses olive oil instead of butter, water or unsalted vegetable stock, more vegetables and less potato.
ingredients: 220 g red lentils, washed and drained
1 small potato, peeled and leached (100 g)
1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp bezar (Saudi spice mix), 1 tsp coriander seeds
1.5 l water or unsalted homemade vegetable stock
1 tbsp lemon juice (15 g) to serve
steps: Dice the potato small, soak it in warm water for 2 hours, then boil it for 5 minutes in plenty of water and drain.
Heat the oil in a pressure cooker and soften the garlic, then the onion, chillies and bell pepper.
Add the spices and coriander seeds, then the lentils, and stir over low heat for 5 minutes.
Add the pumpkin, carrots, tomato, potato, stock and salt, close the cooker and cook for 20–25 minutes on medium heat (or 40 minutes in an ordinary pot).
Take out the chillies if you like, blend the soup until smooth and adjust the thickness with hot water.
Serve hot with a squeeze of lemon.
hints: What changed: olive oil instead of butter, water or unsalted homemade vegetable stock instead of ready stock, and more pumpkin and carrot with only a little leached potato.
Kidney tip: lentils, potato and tomato are sources of potassium and phosphorus; leach the potato as in the first step or replace it with pumpkin, and keep to one bowl.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 36 g carbohydrate and 6 g fibre; serve it with salad and go easy on bread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Mawdoo3

title: Hijazi Baleela
description: Baleela is a popular Hijazi snack, eaten especially in Ramadan: slowly simmered chickpeas served with cumin, vinegar and a quick pickle of beetroot, cucumber and carrot. This version uses no baking soda in the soak, fresh beetroot instead of canned, fresh chilli instead of bottled hot sauce, and little salt.
ingredients: 2 tbsp dark (malt-style) or cider vinegar (30 ml) diluted with 6 tbsp water
steps: Drain and rinse the chickpeas, then put them in a pot with water to cover by 5 cm, the bay leaves and the mint.
Bring to the boil and skim off the foam, then add a splash (about 100 ml) of cold water and skim again; repeat twice.
Turn the heat right down and simmer for 2–3 hours until the chickpeas are tender but whole, adding the salt in the last 30 minutes.
Meanwhile boil the beetroot for 25–30 minutes until tender, then peel and dice it, keeping 3 tbsp of the cooking water.
Mix the beetroot and carrot with the diluted vinegar, lemon juice, beet water and chilli and leave 20 minutes; add the cucumber just before serving.
Ladle the chickpeas with a little of their liquid into small bowls, add the cumin and olive oil, and top with a spoonful of the salad.
hints: What changed: no baking soda in the soak, fresh beetroot instead of canned, fresh chilli instead of salty bottled hot sauce, and little salt.
Kidney tip: chickpeas and beetroot are high in potassium, and chickpeas in phosphorus; keep to one small bowl, drain the chickpeas from their liquid, and you can use less beetroot and more cucumber.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 39 g carbohydrate with 8 g fibre and raises blood sugar slowly; have it as an evening snack in place of sweets.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3 Sufrati, JustFood

title: Qozi with Lamb
description: Qozi is a feast dish in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf: meat is simmered with whole spices, browned in the oven, and served over rice cooked in its stock with pasta, nuts and boiled eggs. This home version uses about 600 g lean lamb leg instead of a whole lamb, a measured amount of rice and whole-wheat pasta, toasted rather than fried almonds, and less ghee and salt.
ingredients: 600 g lean lamb leg (one piece or large pieces)
1 cinnamon stick, 6 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 dried lime (loomi), 2 bay leaves and ½ tsp black peppercorns
1 pinch saffron soaked in 2 tbsp rose water
40 g whole-wheat spaghetti, broken in half
½ tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar) and a pinch of turmeric
1 tomato (100 g) and 1 cucumber (100 g), sliced, and 1 lemon (15 ml juice)
steps: Trim visible fat from the meat, put it in a pot with 1.5 l water, the onion, garlic, carrot and whole spices, bring to the boil skimming the foam, then simmer 1½ hours until tender.
Rinse the rice and soak it for 30 minutes. Lift out the meat, strain the stock and skim the fat off the top.
Heat the oven to 220 °C. Mix the tomato paste with the oil and half the saffron, brush it over the meat, and roast on a tray for 15–20 minutes until browned.

Bring 400 ml of the stock to the boil with the ghee, spices, turmeric and salt, add the drained rice and cook on high heat until the stock is absorbed, then cover and cook on low heat for 20 minutes and drizzle the rest of the saffron on top.
Boil the spaghetti in the remaining stock (or water) until tender and drain.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until lightly golden.

Spread the rice on a serving platter, arrange the pasta around the edges and the sliced meat in the centre, top with the almonds, raisins and boiled eggs, and serve with the tomato, cucumber and lemon.
hints: What changed: lean, trimmed lamb leg, rice and whole-wheat pasta at about 150 g cooked per person, almonds toasted without oil, less ghee, and homemade stock instead of stock cubes.
Kidney tip: meat, egg and almonds contain phosphorus and raisins and tomato paste add potassium; keep to 90 g meat, leave out the raisins, and you can use only the egg whites.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 56 g carbohydrate; start with the salad, and you can swap half the rice for brown rice or bulgur.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Fatafeat, Wikipedia (Quzi)

title: Hijazi Lamb Zirbyan
description: Zirbyan is a rice dish from Aden and Yemen that has long been at home in Makkah and Jeddah: meat and potatoes are marinated in yoghurt, onion, garlic and spices, cooked, then covered with parboiled rice and scented with saffron. This version uses lean leg of lamb, low-fat yoghurt and whole spices instead of a stock cube and ready curry spice, with limited salt and a moderate amount of basmati rice.
ingredients: 600 g lean leg of lamb, cubed, visible fat trimmed
300 g potatoes (2 medium), peeled and halved
2 medium onions (220 g): half an onion grated for the marinade, the rest thinly sliced
1 tsp ground coriander + 1 tsp ground cumin
½ tsp turmeric + ½ tsp black pepper
½ tsp ground cardamom + ½ tsp ground cinnamon
3 cardamom pods + 3 cloves + 1 cinnamon stick + 1 bay leaf
a pinch of saffron soaked in 2 tbsp rose water or warm water
steps: Peel and halve the potatoes, soak them in hot water for 1 hour, then boil them in fresh water for 5 minutes and drain (this lowers the potassium).
Mix the yoghurt with the grated onion, garlic, ginger, vinegar, ground spices and half the salt, and marinate the meat in it for at least 1 hour.
Heat the olive oil in a heavy pot and cook the sliced onion over medium heat until soft and golden brown; lift out half for the topping.
Lift the meat out of the marinade, add it to the pot and stir for 10 minutes until browned, then add the marinade, 250 ml hot water and the rest of the salt.
Cover and simmer for 50–60 minutes until the meat is tender, laying the potatoes on top of the meat for the last 20 minutes. A little thick sauce should remain.
Meanwhile wash the rice and soak it for 20 minutes, then boil it in water with the cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, bay leaf and the pinch of salt for 6–7 minutes until half cooked, and drain.
Spread the rice over the meat and potatoes and sprinkle with the soaked saffron and the remaining browned onion.
Cover the pot tightly and leave on very low heat for 15–20 minutes until the rice is done.
Fold the layers gently when serving and serve with a green salad or a cucumber and low-fat yoghurt salad.
hints: What changed: no stock cube and no salty ready curry spice, 5 g salt for the whole pot, lean meat, low-fat yoghurt, only 2 tbsp oil instead of a lot for frying the onions, and 150 g cooked rice per portion.
Kidney tip: potatoes, meat and yoghurt are sources of potassium and phosphorus; soak and boil the potatoes as in step 1 or swap them for pumpkin or courgette, and keep to one portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 66 g carbohydrate from rice and potatoes; you can swap half the potatoes for courgette or carrot or mix in some brown rice, and start with the salad.
Suitable for: a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia (Zurbian), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Hijazi Vegetable Musaqqaa
description: Musaqqaa as cooked in Hijazi homes: eggplant, potato and carrot with onion and chilli in a thick tomato sauce, served beside rice or bread. Here the vegetables are roasted in the oven with a little olive oil instead of being fried, and the tomato paste is no-salt-added.
ingredients: 2 medium potatoes, peeled and cubed (250 g)
½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp cumin and ½ tsp ground coriander
steps: Soak the potato cubes in warm water for 30 minutes, then drain and pat dry.
Heat the oven to 220 °C. Toss the eggplant, potato and carrot with 1 tbsp of the oil and spread them on a lined tray.
Roast for 25–30 minutes, turning once, until browned and tender.
In a pot heat the rest of the oil and soften the onion and chilli without browning, then add the garlic.
Add the tomato, tomato paste, spices, salt and 100 ml water and cook for 10 minutes until thick.
Add the roasted vegetables, stir gently, cover and simmer 10 minutes to absorb the sauce. Serve hot or warm.
hints: What changed: the vegetables are roasted with a spoon of oil instead of deep-fried, with no-salt tomato paste and little salt.

Kidney tip: potato, tomato and eggplant contain potassium; cut the potatoes small and boil them in plenty of water for 10 minutes, discarding the water, before roasting, or replace them with more eggplant and carrot, and keep to a small plate.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 30 g carbohydrate from the potatoes; if you serve it with rice or bread, halve the rice or bread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty Kitchen, Mawdoo3

title: Hijazi Mantu
description: Mantu are dumplings filled with minced meat and onion and steamed; they are a well-known dish of Bukharan origin in the Hijaz, especially Makkah and Jeddah, served with a yoghurt sauce and a hot tomato sauce. This version uses half wholewheat flour, lean meat, low-fat yoghurt and little salt, and the mantu are steamed, not fried.
ingredients: 2 medium onions (200 g), grated and squeezed
1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp black pepper, ¼ tsp chilli powder
1 tsp olive oil to grease the steamer (4.5 g)
1 garlic clove (4 g), crushed, and ½ tsp dried mint
1 green chilli (10 g) and 1 garlic clove (4 g)
1 tbsp lemon juice (15 ml) and 1 handful fresh coriander (10 g)
steps: Mix both flours with the salt and egg, add the water a little at a time and knead to a soft, smooth dough that does not stick. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Mix the meat well with the squeezed onion, cumin, black pepper, chilli and salt.
Roll the dough out thinly and cut it into 24 squares (about 8 cm). Put a spoon of filling in the middle of each, bring the four corners up over it and pinch well to seal.
Grease the steamer trays with the oil, arrange the mantu with space between them, set them over boiling water, cover and steam for 35–40 minutes until the filling is cooked.
For the yoghurt sauce: mix the yoghurt with the garlic and mint.
For the hot sauce: pulse the tomatoes, chilli, garlic, lemon juice and coriander in a blender until coarse.
Serve the mantu hot with both sauces and a light sprinkle of cumin and black pepper.
hints: What changed: the mantu are steamed, not fried, half the flour is wholewheat, 90% lean meat replaces fatty meat and ghee, the yoghurt is low-fat, and the hot sauce is fresh tomato with no added salt.
Kidney tip: meat, yoghurt and tomato add phosphorus and potassium; eat 4 dumplings instead of 6, have just 2 tbsp of the yoghurt sauce, and swap the tomato in the hot sauce for roasted red pepper.
Diabetes tip: one portion (6 dumplings) has about 48 g carbohydrate; serve it with a large green salad and no extra rice or bread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Layalina Yummy, Mawdoo3

title: Qassimi Fatit
description: Fatit is a traditional Najdi biscuit, famous in Al-Qassim: crumbly round cookies of wholewheat flour with cardamom, ginger and saffron, baked and served with a honey, cinnamon and black lime syrup. This version uses less than a third of the usual sugar, less than half the oil, and skimmed milk powder.
ingredients: 1 pinch saffron soaked in 1 tbsp water (or ¼ tsp turmeric)
steps: Heat the oven to 190°C with top and bottom heat and line two trays with baking paper.
Whisk the egg with the sugar, oil, soaked saffron, cardamom, ginger and salt.
Mix the flour with the milk powder and baking powder, add it to the egg mixture with the water a little at a time, and knead to a firm dough that is easy to shape and does not stick.
Divide the dough into 16 balls and flatten each into a round about 1 cm thick. Press it with a wooden fatit mould, or with a basket or sieve, to make the pattern.
Bake for 15–20 minutes until the edges and bottoms are golden, then cool on a rack.
For the syrup: simmer the water with the honey, cinnamon, cardamom and black lime for 2 minutes until slightly thick, then strain.
Serve each round with 1 tsp of syrup spooned over it or on the side for dipping.
hints: What changed: 60 g sugar instead of about 200 g, 60 ml oil instead of about 180 ml, skimmed milk powder, and a lighter honey syrup in a small amount per round.
Kidney tip: wholewheat flour, milk powder and baking powder contain phosphorus; keep to one round, and you can use low-sodium baking powder and half white flour.
Diabetes tip: one round has about 20 g carbohydrate including 6 g added sugar; have one with unsweetened Arabic coffee and skip the syrup if you can.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia (Fatit), Khaleej Kitchen (Qassim kleicha)

title: Najdi Red Hareis
description: Najdi hareis is whole wheat slow-cooked for hours with meat, tomato and spices, then beaten smooth and topped with an onion kishna; it is popular in Najd and Hail in Ramadan and at Eid. This version uses lean meat, one spoon of oil and a little ghee in the kishna instead of plenty of ghee, no-salt-added tomato paste and little salt.
ingredients: 240 g hareis wheat (whole hulled wheat), washed and soaked 2 hours
600 g lean boneless veal or young camel meat, visible fat removed, cubed
1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), 1 tsp turmeric, ½ tsp ground red pepper, ½ tsp cardamom
steps: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot and cook the onion until soft, then add the meat and spices and brown for 8–10 minutes.
Add the grated tomato and tomato paste and stir for 5 minutes until thick.

Add the drained wheat and boiling water, bring to the boil, then turn the heat very low, cover and cook for 3½–4 hours, stirring now and then and adding boiling water when needed (or 1½ hours in a pressure cooker).
Add the salt in the last hour, then beat the hareis while hot with a wooden masher or hand blender until the meat falls apart and blends with the wheat.
For the kishna: heat the ghee in a small pan and fry the onion until golden, then add the chilli and dried lime for 1 minute.
Spread the hareis in a serving dish, spoon the kishna over the top and serve hot with a green salad.
hints: What changed: lean meat, 1 tbsp oil and 2 tsp ghee for the whole pot instead of plenty of butter and ghee, no-salt-added tomato paste instead of a whole can of tomato sauce, and less salt.

Kidney tip: whole wheat and meat are high in phosphorus, and tomato and tomato paste in potassium; use half the tomato paste, keep to one portion (about 100 g cooked meat) and ask your dietitian about whole grains.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 53 g carbohydrate from fibre-rich whole grain; eat it with salad and do not add sugar on top.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen (hareis with meat and onion), Saudipedia (popular foods of Hail)

title: Bukhari Rice with Chicken
description: Bukhari rice is a well-known Hijazi dish of Makkah, Madinah and Jeddah with roots in Bukhara: basmati rice cooked in spiced chicken broth with carrots, topped with carrots and raisins and served with oven-browned chicken. This version uses skinless chicken, a little olive oil and unsalted tomato paste, with no stock cubes or soy sauce.
ingredients: 300 g skinless chicken breast, in 2 pieces
whole spices: 5 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 bay leaf, ½ tsp black peppercorns
ground Bukhari spice: 1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp coriander, ½ tsp black lime, ¼ tsp cardamom
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked for 30 minutes
2 large carrots (250 g), cut into thin sticks
steps: Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a pot and cook the onion with the whole spices until soft and lightly golden, then add the garlic and orange peel and stir.
Add the chicken and turn it until it changes colour, then add the tomato, tomato paste and a quarter of the carrots and stir for 2 minutes.
Add 800 ml hot water, bring to the boil, then simmer for 25–30 minutes, adding the ground spice for the last 5 minutes.
Lift the chicken onto an oven tray, strain the broth and measure 400 ml.

Return the broth to the pot with the salt; when it boils add the drained rice and half of the remaining carrots. Cook on high until the liquid is absorbed, then cover tightly and leave on very low heat for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile mix 3 tbsp of broth with the turmeric and 1 tsp of the oil, brush it over the chicken and grill at 220°C (top heat) for 10–15 minutes, brushing once or twice, until browned.
Heat the rest of the oil in a frying pan and stir the remaining carrots until soft, then add the raisins for a minute.
Spoon the rice onto a platter, scatter the carrots and raisins around the edge, set the chicken in the middle and serve with a tomato and cucumber salad.
hints: What changed: skinless chicken instead of a whole bird with skin, only 2 tbsp oil, no-salt-added tomato paste, no seasoning powder, soy sauce or sugar on the carrots, and orange peel and black lime for flavour instead of extra salt.
Kidney tip: tomato, tomato paste, raisins and carrots add potassium; use one tomato, cut the raisins to 15 g, and keep to about 90 g cooked chicken per portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 59 g carbohydrate; keep to 150 g cooked rice, you can make half of it brown rice, and serve with a large salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Hia Magazine, Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Qatifi Mahmous with Chicken
description: Mahmous is a rice dish from Qatif, Al-Ahsa and Bahrain, dark brown from a large amount of onion roasted until almost black and from dried black lime, cooked with chicken, meat or fish. Here the onions are caramelised slowly with splashes of water and far less oil, with skinless chicken and little salt and no stock cubes.
ingredients: 600 g skinless chicken (thighs and breasts), cut into 8 pieces
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 30 minutes (about 250 ml)
Whole spices: 1 cinnamon stick, 5 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 2 bay leaves
2 tsp salt-free mixed spice (bezar), ¾ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
steps: Put the onions in a wide heavy pot over medium heat with a splash of water and stir until soft and the water has evaporated.
Add the oil and keep stirring for 25–30 minutes, adding a splash of water whenever it starts to stick, until the onions are very dark brown but not burnt.
Add the whole and ground spices and the garlic and stir for 2 minutes, then add a splash of water and cover for 3 minutes.
Add the chicken and turn it for 10 minutes until coated brown from the onions.
Add the hot water, loomi and salt, cover and simmer for 30 minutes until the chicken is cooked.
Lift the chicken onto a tray and brown it in an oven preheated to 220 °C for 10 minutes without added fat.
Measure the broth: you need about 375 ml. Add the drained rice and boil uncovered without stirring until the broth is absorbed.
Turn the heat to the lowest setting, cover and cook 20 minutes until the rice is done.
Spoon the rice onto a platter, top with the chicken and serve with a green salad and cucumber.
hints: What changed: the onions are roasted in 2 tbsp oil with splashes of water instead of being covered in oil, the chicken is skinless and browned in the oven, there are no stock cubes, and the rice portion is about 150 g cooked per person.
Kidney tip: chicken is high in phosphorus and potassium; keep to one plate (about 100 g cooked chicken). The dish has no tomato or potato, so it is lighter in potassium than many rice dishes.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 54 g carbohydrate; serve with a large salad, and you can mix in a quarter brown rice.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Wikipedia, Cookinsta

title: Shakshouka
description: Saudi shakshouka is a common home breakfast: onion, garlic, tomato and green chilli are cooked with cumin into a thick sauce, then eggs are stirred in until set and it is eaten with bread. This version uses a little olive oil, less salt, some egg whites in place of whole eggs, and more vegetables.
ingredients: 4 whole eggs (200 g) and 2 egg whites (66 g)
2 green chillies (20 g) and 1 small green bell pepper (100 g), chopped
½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp bezar, a pinch of black pepper
steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide pan and cook the onion until soft, then add the garlic, chillies and bell pepper and stir for 2 minutes.
Stir in the cumin and bezar, then add the tomatoes, tomato paste and 50 ml water and cover for 8–10 minutes until the sauce is thick.
Whisk the whole eggs with the egg whites, salt and black pepper and pour them over the sauce.
Stir gently on low heat now and then until the eggs are set as you like, then sprinkle with coriander and serve hot with whole-wheat bread.
hints: What changed: 1 tbsp olive oil for the whole pan, less salt, 2 of the eggs replaced by whites to lower cholesterol, and more vegetables.
Kidney tip: tomatoes and tomato paste are high in potassium and egg yolk contains phosphorus; you can cut the tomatoes to 2 with more peppers, and use more egg whites.
Diabetes tip: shakshouka is low in carbohydrate and high in protein; the carbohydrate comes from the bread, so have half a whole-wheat flatbread.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, vegetarians, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Sayidaty, Layalina Yummy

title: Goat Mufattah (Home Version)
description: Mufattah is Saudi Arabia's feast dish of generosity: a whole lamb or goat cooked and served on rice. This is a scaled-down home version with about 600 g of lean goat instead of a whole animal, no stock cubes, little ghee and a salad without fried bread.
ingredients: 600 g goat leg and shoulder on the bone, visible fat trimmed (edible meat weight)
Whole spices: 2 dried limes, 1 cinnamon stick, 5 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, 2 bay leaves; plus 1 tsp bezar
For the glaze: 1 egg (50 g) beaten with 3 tbsp of the broth and a pinch of saffron and turmeric
200 g basmati rice, washed and soaked 20 minutes
1 tbsp olive oil (13.5 g) and 2 tsp ghee (9 g)
¾ tsp salt (4 g), split between meat and rice
1 tbsp lemon juice (15 g) and sumac
steps: Put the goat in a pot with the water, bring to the boil and skim, then add the onion, tomato, whole spices, bezar and ¼ tsp of the salt.
Simmer for 1½–2 hours until tender (or 45 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Lift the meat onto an oven tray, strain the broth, let it settle and skim off the fat.
Beat the egg with 3 tbsp broth, saffron and turmeric, brush it over the meat and brown under the top heat of the oven at 220°C for 15 minutes.
In a pot, soften the onion in the oil and ghee, add the tomato and carrot, then the drained rice, the rest of the salt and 450 ml of the strained broth.
When it boils, cover and simmer 15–20 minutes until done. You can smoke the rice and meat with a glowing piece of charcoal in a metal bowl for 3 minutes.
Toss the salad ingredients with the lemon juice and sumac, without salt or fried bread.
Spread the rice on a large platter, place the meat on top and serve with the salad.
hints: What changed: a home version with about 600 g meat instead of a whole goat, no stock cubes, fat skimmed from the broth, little ghee, a salad without fried bread and no fried liver or offal.
Kidney tip: with its salad this plate is high in potassium (meat, tomato, carrot, leafy greens); use less tomato and rocket and keep to 90–100 g cooked meat.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 54 g carbohydrate; start with the salad and skip dessert after the meal.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Saudipedia (Kabsa and Mufattah), Sayidaty Kitchen

title: Qassimi Tawa
description: Tawa (also taawa or manafeekh) is a traditional winter breakfast from Qassim and Najd: small rounds of risen whole-wheat dough with nigella seeds that puff up as they cook, served with honey or date syrup and tea or milk. Here the rounds are baked in a hot oven or a non-stick pan instead of deep-fried, with low-fat laban, half the sugar and a measured amount of honey.
steps: Mix both flours with the sugar, yeast, nigella seeds and salt.
Add the egg, oil and warm laban and knead to a soft, smooth dough, adding a spoon of water if needed; cover and leave to rise for 1 hour.
Heat the oven to 240 °C with a cast-iron tray or baking stone inside.
Divide the dough into 16 small balls and press each one by hand into a thin round about 10 cm wide.

Brush the rounds lightly with oil and bake on the hot tray for 5–6 minutes, turning halfway, until puffed and golden. (You can also cook them in a covered non-stick pan over medium heat for 2 minutes per side.)
Stack the rounds on a plate, pour the honey over and serve hot.
hints: What changed: baked or pan-cooked instead of deep-fried, two-thirds whole-wheat flour, low-fat laban, half the usual sugar in the dough, and limited honey (about 2 tsp per portion).
Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour and laban contain phosphorus and potassium; you can use more white flour and keep to 2 rounds.
Diabetes tip: one portion (2 rounds) has about 37 g carbohydrate; skip the honey and serve with a boiled egg or low-fat labneh and cucumber.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Arabic Wikipedia (Saudi cuisine: tawa), Cookpad Saudi Arabia

title: Meat Muqalqal
description: Muqalqal is a quick Hijazi dish from western Saudi Arabia in which cubes of meat are tossed over high heat with onion, tomato, peppers and spices. This version uses lean lamb leg instead of lamb fat, liver and kidneys, with a little olive oil, less salt and more vegetables.
serving_size: 1 plate (about 250 g), without rice or bread
ingredients: 560 g boneless lamb leg, fat trimmed, cut in 2 cm cubes
1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), ½ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp black pepper
2 tbsp lemon juice (30 g), 2 green chillies (20 g), 2 tbsp water, ½ garlic clove
steps: Heat a heavy deep pan or saj over high heat, add half the oil and toss half the meat for 3–4 minutes until browned, then take it out and repeat with the rest.
Add the remaining oil and the onion and stir until soft, then the garlic, cumin, bezar, turmeric and black pepper for 1 minute.
Return the meat to the pan, add the tomatoes and stir until they start to break down.
Cover and cook on low heat for 30–35 minutes until the meat is tender, stirring now and then and adding 50–100 ml hot water if needed.
Add the bell pepper, chilli and salt and toss over high heat for 4–5 minutes until most of the sauce has cooked down and the pepper is still slightly crisp.
Blend the dip ingredients, then serve the muqalqal sprinkled with coriander, with the dip and a green salad.
hints: What changed: no lamb fat, liver or kidneys (high in cholesterol and phosphorus), lean meat, a little olive oil, about half the usual salt and more peppers and tomato.

Kidney tip: meat and tomatoes are high in potassium and phosphorus; keep to the portion (about 90–100 g cooked meat), and you can halve the tomatoes and add more bell pepper. Ask your dietitian about your own portion.
Diabetes tip: the nutrition values are for the muqalqal alone, without rice or bread; serve it with 150 g cooked rice (adds about 40 g carbohydrate) or one small whole-wheat bread and a large salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, a gluten-free diet.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Sayidaty Kitchen, Eeina (Saudi mugalgal)

title: Southern Aseeda with Marag
description: Southern aseeda is a traditional dish from the south of Saudi Arabia (Asir, Jazan and Al Baha): a thick whole-wheat dough beaten into boiling water with a wooden stick and served hot with meat broth (marag). This version uses lean trimmed lamb, more vegetables in the broth, and less salt and ghee.
ingredients: 520 g lean lamb (leg or shoulder), trimmed, in large pieces
2 carrots (150 g) and 1 large zucchini (200 g), in large pieces
1 cinnamon stick, 4 cardamom pods, 1 bay leaf, ½ tsp black pepper
To sprinkle: ground dried red chilli, cumin and a pinch of garlic powder
steps: Put the meat in a pot with the water, onion, garlic, chilli and whole spices, bring to the boil and skim off the foam.
Lower the heat, cover and cook for 1½ hours until nearly tender, then add the carrots, zucchini, tomato and salt and cook for 20 minutes more.
For the aseeda: boil the 300 ml water with the pinch of salt in a non-stick pot, add the flour all at once and stir fast with a wooden stick or spoon until it forms one mass.
Add 100 ml of the hot broth gradually and keep beating (folding and pressing from the bottom up) on low heat for 10 minutes until smooth and firm.
Shape it in serving bowls, make a well in the centre and put a little ghee in it.
Serve at once with the meat, vegetables and broth, and sprinkle the spices over the broth to taste.
hints: What changed: lean meat instead of fatty ribs and shoulder, vegetables in the broth, and less ghee and salt; the honey-and-ghee version is best kept for occasions and small amounts.

Kidney tip: whole-wheat flour and meat contain phosphorus (about 520 mg per portion) and the broth carries potassium; drink only a little broth, and you can make the aseeda with half white flour to lower phosphorus.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 54 g carbohydrate with 9 g fibre from the whole wheat; serve it with green salad and avoid adding honey.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, WebTeb, Food2mins

title: Qassimi Maraheef with Kishna
description: Maraheef are thin wholewheat flatbreads poured onto a hot griddle (saj), a traditional dish of Qassim and Najd served savoury with kishna or sweet with ghee and honey. This version uses wholewheat flour and yeast instead of baking powder, no sugar, and an onion-tomato kishna made with olive oil, a little ghee and little salt.
ingredients: 1 tsp olive oil to grease the griddle (4.5 g)
½ tsp ground dried lime (loomi), ½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp mixed Saudi spices (bezar), ¼ tsp black pepper
steps: Blend the maraheef ingredients (both flours, egg, milk powder, yeast, salt and water) until smooth and pourable like a thick soup; add a little water if it is too heavy.
Cover the batter and leave it to rest for 30 minutes in a warm place.
For the kishna: heat the olive oil and ghee in a pan and cook the onion over medium heat for 8–10 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the chilli and spices, then the tomatoes and tomato paste; stir and simmer gently for 10 minutes until thick without adding water, then add the salt and spring onion and take off the heat.
Heat a griddle or non-stick pan and wipe it with a little oil on kitchen paper, then pour a small ladle of batter and spread it thinly in a circle with the back of the ladle.
Cook until the top is dry and full of holes (about 1 minute), then turn for 30 seconds; repeat with the rest of the batter (16–20 rounds).
Layer the maraheef in a dish with the hot kishna between and on top, and serve straight away.
hints: What changed: wholewheat instead of white flour, yeast instead of baking powder (which is high in sodium), no sugar in the batter, and a kishna made with 1 tbsp oil and 1 tsp ghee instead of plenty of ghee, with little salt.
Kidney tip: wholewheat flour, tomatoes, tomato paste and milk powder add phosphorus and potassium; you can use half white and half brown flour, cut the tomatoes to 200 g and keep to one portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 48 g carbohydrate; eat it with a green salad or low-fat laban and avoid adding honey or sugar on top.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Saudipedia (popular foods of Qassim), Qassimy Kitchen (maraheef recipe)

title: Madina Date Haysa
description: Haysa is a traditional Madinah sweet of whole-wheat flour toasted in ghee and mixed with dates, cardamom and sesame, served warm with Arabic coffee. We used about a quarter of the usual fat, no added sugar as the dates sweeten it, and shaped it into small pieces.
ingredients: 250 g soft pitted dates (such as Khalas)
10 g toasted sesame seeds (1 tbsp) and ½ tsp nigella seeds
steps: Melt the ghee in a non-stick pot over low heat, add the flour and stir constantly for 6–8 minutes until toasted, golden and fragrant.
Stir in the cardamom, then add the dates and mash them into the flour with a wooden spoon or masher over very low heat until evenly blended (about 5 minutes).
Add the sesame and nigella seeds and stir for 1 minute.
Let it cool slightly, then shape into 12 small balls or squares with damp hands and serve warm with Arabic coffee.
hints: What changed: 25 g ghee instead of 100 g butter plus oil, whole-wheat flour, no added sugar or cream, and small fixed pieces.
Kidney tip: dates are high in potassium (about 170 mg per piece) and sesame and whole-wheat flour contain phosphorus; have one piece, and you can use white flour and skip the sesame.
Diabetes tip: one piece has about 22 g carbohydrate from dates and flour; keep to one piece with coffee after a meal.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (encyclopediacooking.com), Al Bilad Daily, Cookpad

title: Ma'soub
description: Ma'soub is a well-known Hijazi breakfast from Makkah, Jeddah and Madinah: chopped wheat bread tossed with banana and ghee and topped with cream and honey. In this version the bread is made from whole-wheat flour, with little ghee and light cream, and bananas and dates provide most of the sweetness with only a spoon of honey.
steps: Knead the flour with the yeast, salt and water to a soft dough; cover and let it rise for 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 3 balls, roll each one thin and cook in a dry non-stick pan or on a hot saj for 1–2 minutes per side until cooked and spotted.
Cut up the bread and pulse it in a food processor to fine crumbs.
Melt the ghee in a pot over low heat, add the dates and mash until they melt, then add the bread crumbs and toss for 5 minutes.
Add the sliced bananas and cardamom and mash with the spoon while stirring for 3–5 minutes until the mixture is even and soft.
Spoon the ma'soub into serving plates and top each with a teaspoon of cream and a little honey; serve warm.
hints: What changed: home-made whole-wheat bread, much less ghee, a small amount of light cream, and sweetness mainly from bananas and dates with only one spoon of honey for the whole dish.
Kidney tip: bananas and dates are rich in potassium and whole-wheat flour contains phosphorus; use 2 bananas instead of 3 plus a cooked grated apple, and have half a portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 65 g carbohydrate; have half a portion with a boiled egg or low-fat laban and skip the honey.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Mawdoo3, Khaleeji Food

title: Ghamdi Daghabees
description: Daghabees is a traditional dish of the Ghamid and Zahran lands in Al-Baha, southern Saudi Arabia: wheat dough dumplings cooked in meat broth and eaten by hand, pressing a hollow with the thumb and filling it with broth. This version uses lean lamb and whole wheat flour, adds vegetables to the broth, and leaves out stock cubes.
serving_size: 1 plate (about 3 daghabees with meat and broth, 450 g)
ingredients: 560 g lean boneless lamb leg, fat trimmed, cut into large pieces
1 medium zucchini, diced (150 g) and 1 medium carrot, diced (100 g)
1½ tsp cumin, ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp turmeric, a pinch of cinnamon
6 cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick, 1 pierced dried black lime
¾ tsp salt (4.5 g) for the whole recipe, split between broth and dough
steps: Mix both flours with a quarter of the salt, add the warm water gradually and knead to a firm, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Heat the oil in a wide pot, add the cumin, cardamom pods and cinnamon, then the lamb, and brown it on all sides.
Add the onion and garlic and stir for 3 minutes, then the tomatoes, black pepper, turmeric and black lime.
Pour in the hot water, cover leaving a small gap and simmer for 1 hour until the meat is nearly tender, skimming off foam and fat.
Add the zucchini, carrot and the rest of the salt.
With wet hands divide the dough into 12 balls and flatten each in your palm into a thick oval.
Lower the discs into the simmering broth one at a time, leaving a minute between each so they do not stick together.
Cover and simmer 25–30 minutes, gently shaking the pot every 5 minutes, until the dumplings and meat are cooked.
Arrange the daghabees and meat on a platter with the broth and vegetables in a bowl, and dip the dumplings into the broth to eat.
hints: What changed: no stock cubes (common recipes add two and a half), lean lamb with the fat skimmed off the broth, more whole wheat than white flour, and vegetables added to the broth.
Kidney tip: tomato, brown flour and meat add potassium and phosphorus; use more white flour if you need to limit phosphorus, and keep to three dumplings with a little broth.
Diabetes tip: one plate has about 57 g carbohydrate, mostly from the dough; keep to three small dumplings and serve with a green salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Arabic Wikipedia, Al Jawhara Magazine

title: Jazani Marsa
description: Marsa is a traditional dish from the Jazan region: a thin bread baked on a griddle or in the mifa oven is chopped fine and kneaded with mashed banana, then served with ghee and honey, often next to fish. This version uses part whole-wheat flour, only two teaspoons of oil in the dough, and half the usual ghee and honey.
ingredients: 120 g whole-wheat flour and 80 g white flour
steps: Mix both flours with the salt and oil, add the water gradually and knead to a soft dough; rest it for 15 minutes.
Divide the dough into 3 pieces, roll each thin and cook in a non-stick pan over medium heat on both sides until golden and slightly crisp.
While hot, chop the breads very fine or pulse them in a food processor.
Mash the bananas with a fork in a bowl, add the chopped bread and knead together until even.
Press the marsa into a serving dish and smooth the top, pour over the melted ghee, drizzle with the honey and divide into 4 portions.
hints: What changed: part whole-wheat flour, a little oil in the dough instead of lots of fat, about half the usual ghee and honey, and the banana gives most of the sweetness.
Kidney tip: banana is high in potassium (about 90 g banana per portion); you can use one banana only, or all white flour, and keep to one portion.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 56 g carbohydrate; serve it with a piece of grilled fish (it is traditionally eaten with fish) and a green salad, and you can reduce or skip the honey.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Al-Madina newspaper, Cookpad

title: Jazani Haysiya
description: Haysiya is a traditional dish from the Jazan region: sour fermented lahoh bread is torn into a clay bowl (the haysiya), soaked with spiced meat broth and topped with the meat; coastal families call it marshoosh. This version uses lean lamb, whole-grain sorghum and wheat flour for the lahoh, very little ghee, and less salt with no stock cubes.
ingredients: 2 tbsp grated onion (30 g) and 1 crushed garlic clove
560 g lean boneless lamb leg, fat trimmed, cut into medium pieces
1 tsp cumin, ½ tsp black pepper, ½ tsp ground cardamom, a pinch of cinnamon
Whole spices: 2 cloves, 3 cardamom pods, 1 small cinnamon stick
¾ tsp salt (4.5 g) for the whole recipe
2 tsp ghee (8 g) and chopped parsley (10 g) to serve
steps: Mix the sorghum flour, wheat flour, yeast, grated onion and garlic, then whisk in the warm water gradually to a pourable batter like cake batter.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 3–4 hours until bubbly and slightly sour.
Meanwhile heat the oil in a pot and cook the sliced onion until soft and golden, then add the garlic and tomatoes and stir for 3 minutes.

Add the lamb and turn until it changes colour, then add the whole and ground spices and the water. Bring to the boil, lower the heat, cover and simmer 1½ hours until tender, skimming off foam and fat.
Add the salt during the last 10 minutes of cooking.

Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat without oil, pour in a small ladle of batter and spread it into a round. Cook until covered with holes and dry on top, without flipping (about 2 minutes). Repeat to make about 8 rounds.
Tear 2 lahoh rounds into each bowl, ladle the hot broth over them until soaked, then place the meat on top.
Melt the ghee and drizzle ½ tsp over each bowl, sprinkle with parsley and serve hot with a green salad.
hints: What changed: trimmed lamb leg instead of fatty meat, the fat is skimmed from the broth, only 2 tsp ghee for the whole pot instead of a generous pour, little salt with no stock cubes or salted spice mixes, and the lahoh is made from whole grains.

Kidney tip: tomato, meat and whole grains add potassium and phosphorus; keep to one bowl, use one ladle of broth rather than drinking the extra, and you can swap half the whole wheat flour for white flour to lower phosphorus.
Diabetes tip: one bowl has about 45 g carbohydrate from the lahoh; whole sorghum and wheat raise blood sugar more slowly than white bread, so serve it with a large salad.
Suitable for: people with diabetes, heart health and blood pressure.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking (Mawsouat Al Tabkh), Sayidaty Kitchen, Yummy (Layalina)

title: Pumpkin Luqaimat
description: Pumpkin luqaimat are a Gulf and Saudi take on luqaimat in which pumpkin purée and yoghurt go into the dough with saffron and cardamom; they are usually deep-fried and dipped in sugar syrup. Here they are cooked in an aebleskiver (round pancake) pan or air fryer with a little olive oil, half the flour is whole wheat, and a little date syrup replaces the sugar syrup.
ingredients: ½ tsp ground cardamom and a pinch of saffron
steps: Boil the pumpkin in a little water for 12–15 minutes until soft, then drain well and let it cool slightly.
Blend the pumpkin with the yoghurt and water until smooth.
In a large bowl mix both flours, the cornflour, yeast, salt, cardamom and saffron, then add the pumpkin mixture and beat hard by hand or with a spoon to a soft, sticky dough.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 to 1½ hours until doubled.

Heat an aebleskiver (round pancake) pan over medium heat, brush the hollows lightly with oil and drop a small ball of dough into each with two wet spoons; turn until browned all over and cooked through (4–5 minutes). Or air-fry in an oiled basket at 190 °C for 8–10 minutes, shaking once.
Pile the luqaimat on a plate, drizzle with the date syrup, sprinkle with sesame and serve at once.
hints: What changed: no deep frying (one spoon of olive oil for the whole batch), half whole-wheat flour, low-fat yoghurt, and a little date syrup instead of sugar syrup.
Kidney tip: pumpkin, date syrup, yoghurt and whole-wheat flour contain potassium and phosphorus; keep to 6 pieces, and you can use all white flour and less syrup.
Diabetes tip: one portion has about 47 g carbohydrate; have 3 pieces with no syrup or just 1 tsp, with Arabic coffee instead of sweet tea.
Suitable for: heart health and blood pressure, kidney disease (not on dialysis), people on dialysis, vegetarians.
References: Encyclopedia Cooking, Fatafeat, Cookpad Saudi Arabia
